utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. Paul Rogers appearing for the Prosecution together with my team, Priya Gopalan, Ms. Daniela Kravetz, Ms. Barbara Goy, and Mr. Aditya Menon, and our case manager today Mr. Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence, starting with Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ben Emmerson on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, together with my learned friends Rod Dixon and Ms. Annie O'Reilly and Mr. Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, Gregor Guy-Smith appearing on behalf of Mr. Balaj with Ms. Colleen Rohan and Mr. Chad Mair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Richard Harvey appearing for Mr. Brahimaj, together with Mr. Paul Troop, Ms. Sophie Rigney, and Mr. Luke Boenisch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all you should have a bundle of documents which we have produced which are copies of the slides that we will be showing during the course of the opening this afternoon. Your Honours, sometimes it's easier to see them in the hard copy than on the small screens because I know that there is variable quality sometimes on the screen itself, and so that's why we have produced them I hope to be of some assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the crimes alleged in this partial re-trial cover a short time-frame, between about the 19th of May, 1998, and approximately the end of July 1998. The crimes for which these accused are to be held criminally responsible in this trial were, the Prosecution says, all perpetrated in the KLA prison at Jabllanice in the municipality of Gjakove, western Kosovo. Your Honours, the counts allege murder, torture, and cruel treatment against the laws and customs of war. They were comitted pursuant to a joint criminal enterprise involving the three accused, Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj, in which we say collaborators, spies, and those suspected of treachery or opposition to the KLA were targeted. The victims were beaten, tortured, and in some cases murdered, regardless of their ethnicity, be they Serb, Roma, Egyptian/Ashkali, or Kosovar Albanian, whether they were Christian or Muslim. And in relation to Counts 1 and Count 6 involved, say the Prosecution, the direct participation of all three accused. The crimes charged in this indictment occurred in the context of an armed conflict which existed from and including the 22nd of April, 1998, throughout Kosovo, between Serbian armed forces and the Kosovo Liberation Army, of which all three accused were leaders. The Kosovo Liberation Army was fighting what it considered was a war of liberation, as its name implies. The accused pursued that aim, and in so doing sought to control, to the exclusion of enemy forces, the area defined in the indictment as the Dukagjin Operational Zone, forming part of the municipalities of Decani or Decan, Pec Peje, Djakovica Gjakove, and Klina, Kline. And, Your Honours, I will adopt simply for ease of reference the Albanian version of the towns' names to avoid having to repeat them all the time. And, Your Honours, they did this by suppressing real or perceived opposition. While they were fighting a war and thus using legitimate force, they also pursued illegal means to achieve their aim: They mistreated civilians who were or were perceived to be opposing the KLA. This case is about the implementation of the common purpose in the village of Jabllanice in the Gjakove municipality. Your Honours, I'd first like to orientate the Chamber, if I may, as to some of the geography in the area the subject of the indictment. Your Honours, showing on your screen now is a slide of the whole of Kosovo, and Your Honours can see that it shows all the municipalities and it also shows the national boundaries -- Your Honours, I hope it's on your screen. I'm grateful. It also shows the national boundaries. Your Honours can see starting in the -- on the right-hand side of the page Serbia and then going down south to Macedonia, across to the west, to Albania, and north then into Montenegro. And Your Honours can see to the west of Kosovo on the borders with Montenegro and Albania, starting in the north, the municipality of Pec, you can see the town of Pec really forming the centre of that municipality slide. Moving south into Decan and the town of Decani marked just in pink. And moving forward south from there to Gjakove and the town Gjakove marked at the bottom in the centre, rather, of that municipality. And then if we travel north from Gjakove, you will find the municipality of Kline. And what is not shown on this particular side is there is a road - and I will show you the next slide in a moment - there is a road which joins Gjakove and Kline. Your Honours, the area of Kosovo is about a quarter of the size of the Netherlands, with a population of approximately 2 million. And Your Honours can see from this municipality map that the area that we're concerned with is within about a quarter of the size of Kosovo itself. So we say it's a relatively small area that we're dealing with. Can I show you now the next map. Your Honour, this is a map that the Prosecution have put together to try to identify or at least highlight the main towns and villages that you'll be hearing about. One of the problems with the more detailed topographical maps is they're very crowded with lots of contour lines, and it's hard to see sometimes where everything is. But just to orientate you around this map, if I may, starting on the left-hand side of the map to the top left-hand corner you'll see the town of Peje. And then if we travel along the red road, and these are the main roads we say that are linking the main towns, we travel along the main road to the east. Imagine yourselves driving along through Zahac, down to Zajmovo, which is marked by the rivers, in conjunction with the rivers, and then just a little north to Kline. Then there's the village of Dolac and then we get back in the car and drive south, passing Dolovo, carrying on the road and passing the Lake Radoniq and then arriving in Gjakove. Pausing briefly in Gjakove to point the car back towards Peja and drive up to Decani. And on the way to Decan on the right you will see the village of Gllogjan. That is the village in which Mr. Haradinaj has his family home and which forms one of the headquarters, we say, of the KLA in this case, not to be confused with another Gllogjan, which is a Catholic village of Gllogjan, and I'll identify where that is very shortly. Your Honours, very broadly, we say, that within the red road area, the KLA had through the indictment period substantial control of that area. Outside the red road area and along them represented areas of conflict with Serb forces. Now, Your Honour, that's not to say that there was no conflict within the areas bounded by the roads, particularly in the west around Mr. Haradinaj's villages and in the Lake Radoniq area, but that the Prosecution says the KLA had a broad measure of control in that central area. Your Honours, can I take you back to the village of Zajmovo just south of Kline, back on the road there, and you'll see just to the west of Zajmovo on the other side of the river a village called Grabanice. And Your Honours will hear a reasonable amount of evidence about the events in Grabanice. Travelling south-west from Grabanice, we come to Catholic Gllogjan, and south of Catholic Gllogjan is Jabllanice, which will form really the main centre-piece for the evidence that you'll be hearing during this case. And then south-west of Jabllanice is the village of Zhabel, which you will also hear something about. You can take the map off, please. Your Honours, can I deal now a little with what the Prosecution says is the evidence relating to the development of the KLA in this area, the road-bounded area which broadly we call the Dukagjin area. Your Honours, I will then, after I have dealt with that, turn to the development -- first deal with the geographical control, forgive me, and then I will turn to the development of the organisation of the KLA within the Dukagjin area and address the consolidation of what we say is Ramush Haradinaj's control of the KLA within that area. Dealing first, if I may, with geographical control. Your Honours, the first two KLA headquarters established in the Dukagjin were firstly in Jabllanice, in the Gjakove municipality, the oldest headquarters in western Kosovo, and under the control of Lahi Brahimaj, also known as Maxhup, or Gypsy, and he was Ramush and is Ramush Haradinaj's maternal uncle. And secondly, in the village of Gllogjan, in Decan, under the control of Mr. Haradinaj, also known as Smajl. Your Honours, in 1998, Colonel John Crosland was the British military attache to the embassy in Belgrade. He produced the map in the last trial to show the area known as the Dukagjin between March and May 1998. Your Honours, if I can show you, please, that map that he produced in the trial. He described the black line which overlaps in part of the blue as showing the boundary of this area and said that throughout Kosovo there was several groupings of the KLA and in particular of this area of the Dukagjin. He marked the blue line to show the Peje to Decani road as a place where he described were "shoot and scoot tactics," that's the phrase that he used, employed by the KLA against Serbian forces in the early part of the conflict. The road he described had become a thin red line or a front line for Serbian forces, who were trying to prevent the flow of men and materials from Albania where the Kosovo Liberation Army was arming itself, into Kosovo itself. And Your Honours will recall from the first map that I showed you how close to the borders of Albania and indeed Montenegro these municipalities are. Serb forces, he said, had been unable to hold the mountainous area along the Albanian border and had fallen back effectively along this road, and he described many battles being fought along and around the road. And Your Honours will note from this map that the village of Gllogjan, Ramush Haradinaj's village and the headquarters, is within the cluster of circles immediately to the right of the bottom half of the blue line. In fact, you can see two rather poorly formed blue circles, and just to the right of those rather poorly formed blue circles is a circle and in there is the village of Gllogjan. On a larger-scale map it's clearer to see, but I think Your Honours have the general picture. Your Honours will find all these maps in your bundle and in the bundle it's at page 3. Your Honours, as the KLA grew during 1998, it began to establish control of parts of the territory of Kosovo. And in relation to this indictment, by April to May 1998 the KLA in the Dukagjin area had established what we describe and others have described as a free area, substantially free of Serb control. Again, I make it clear that does not mean there were not attacks and incursions, but nevertheless substantially the area was under KLA control. And Colonel Crosland, again in the first trial, drew a map to indicate this area of control between about March and June/July 1998. And again broadly you can see that the area marked in red inside the boundaries of the three roads, and this is the area that Colonel Crosland indicated, and you can see in there written KLA, was what he described as basically a KLA area, and the Serbs would stay on the outside and attempt to dominate and influence areas by shelling into that area. He said: "... the Serbs took up a position that they could, if you like, contain the fighters within this area by dominating the roads ... so Serbian security forces would go off the road a short way, make a raid, re-arrange a few houses rather badly," as he put it, "and then withdraw back out because they did not feel safe in that area." And, Your Honours, that's the 65 ter number 04022, and it's a transcript reference at page 3029. Indeed, Your Honours can see that Colonel Crosland's map shows in blue pockets of Serb forces along the road area, including near the southern part of Lake Radoniq and inside that area and in and around the high ground to the south of that area. And whilst there were incursions into the area and indeed later full-scale assaults by Serb forces, the Prosecution says broadly this was the zone of influence and control established by the KLA with the Serbs on the outside. Your Honours, in addition you will hear evidence from Nebojsa Avramovic, who was a police officer working as a crime technician in the Djakovica SUP, a part of the Ministry of the Interior forces, the Serbian police. He'd been in that position since 1996, and he produces a map as an annex to his statement of roads that were regarded as unsafe by Serb police between April and September 1998. Your Honours should have that I think on the screen now. And Your Honours will see three markings, three coloured markings, A, B, and C. C represents the road from Djakovica to Prizren at the bottom of the map, Djakovica being at the bottom. I hope Your Honours are now becoming familiar with what is really a triangle of roads running between Djakovica, Peje, and Kline. And at the bottom is Djakovica. The road running from Djakovica to Prizren marked C he said was a road that was free to travel upon. If it's easier for Your Honours, it's at page 5 of the map bundle. It may be a little bit clearer, actually, there, but anyway. The area marked A, the portion of the Djakovica to Kline road which is marked A, he said was safe for Serb police to travel upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is -- where is A? Is it on the left corner of the triangle?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It's on the -- yes, it's on the left-hand -- the right-hand road, forgive me, running between Djakovica and Kline. It's a little unclear, but it's marked in orange or red. Does Your Honour have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the section of the road running from Djakovica to Kline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the safe area?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: That's the safe area. And if Your Honour remembers the map I've just shown you where there were Serb forces noted by Colonel Crosland in that southern part of this area, that may have some correlation between those two things. But north of that in the area marked B, the witness describes that being -- as an area which he says was completely blocked by the KLA from April to September 1998. That was his statement. And, Your Honour, we say it is significant that in that area marked B two of the victims in the indictment were abducted. They were Witness 6 and Nenad Remistar, a Serb traffic police officer. I should indicate, Your Honours, that the map -- this map isn't presently on the 65 ter list because it was omitted from -- by accident from Mr. Avramovic's statement. I will move in due course to admit it formally, but I mention that now in case so there's -- in case my learned friends are trying to find it. It has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Nowhere is it part of the 65 ter statement with regard to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It is. We'll deal with that later. Your Honours, the Prosecution, moving on, says it can be seen by looking at Colonel Crosland's maps, assessing his evidence, and looking at other maps and evidence produced by KLA commanders and Serb commanders there is a general consensus about the broad areas of control established by KLA forces between April and September 1998 and broad agreement as to where the confrontation lines ran. Essentially there was a free area in which the KLA had greater freedom to operate away from the confrontation lines. Your Honours, turning now to organisational development of the KLA. Your Honours, Colonel Crosland described the KLA in the early part of 1998 as a fledgling organisation. Your Honours, the evidence will show that during the period between March 1998 and September 1998 the KLA was developing into a more organised force, from village-based commands to more regional commands, and a more military-style hierarchical leadership. KLA witnesses including Rrustem Tetaj, Jakup Krasniqi show that between March and April 1998, villagers in many villages in the Dukagjin area began to organise themselves in support of the KLA into defence units, often electing a village commander, appointing guards, and setting up check-points at village entrances. The KLA also had a General Staff, but at least until June 1998 the General Staff had no main building. All three accused were commanders within the KLA. Ramush Haradinaj, based in Gllogjan; Lahi Brahimaj, based in Jabllanice; and Idriz Balaj, who had moved from Jabllanice to Gllogjan and had been appointed as commander of a special unit known as the Black Eagles by Ramush Haradinaj. Just as the KLA, Your Honours, began to consolidate its control over the Dukagjin area, so too Ramush Haradinaj consolidated his control over the KLA. Your Honours, it's significant, the Prosecution says, that Ramush Haradinaj, together with his maternal uncle, Lahi Brahimaj, had been at the forefront of the development of the KLA in the Dukagjin area since the earliest days of the KLA as a movement in 1994. In the Dukagjin area, the subject of the indictment, the Prosecution says the organisation of the KLA was greatly assisted by the two main headquarters being within the same extended family. Gllogjan, controlled by Ramush Haradinaj, and Jabllanice by Lahi Brahimaj, his maternal uncle. Within the Kosovar Albanian clan-based culture, the Prosecution says these familial ties have great significance. Indeed, witnesses describe being married not just to an individual but to an entire village. The Prosecution says it's quite clear that these familial ties lay at the heart of the initial organisation of the Dukagjin Zone and its headquarters. In a compilation of interviews with Ramush Haradinaj entitled "A Narrative About War and Freedom" --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think Mr. Rogers is aware, because I indicated to him in advance, that I would at this stage rise because he is about to seek to present, we say again misleadingly, to the Trial Chamber a document which he suggests is a series of interviews but is in fact a book published by a journalist called Bardh Hamzaj. There is no evidence - and the Prosecution has none - from the author of this book as to the provenance of the contents. There is no evidence as to the source of the descriptions or statements he attributes to Ramush Haradinaj. There is nothing to suggest that the book was authorised or ever adopted by Ramush Haradinaj or written with his authority. And for that reason, the previous Trial Chamber, rightly, regarded it as worthless evidence and excluded it on the basis it was impossible to understand what ought to be clear as to its provenance or to be in a position to distinguish between truth, falsity, hyperbole, or fact, propaganda, or accurate reporting and that there was nothing to corroborate it. So that before Mr. Rogers again, I say misleadingly, launches into the suggestion that this is a record of interview, it's rights right that Your Honours should know it is nothing of the sort, it is again forensic rubbish, and it's material about which there is an outstanding application of exclusion in which the Defence rely precisely the same arguments that persuaded the previous Trial Chamber to throw it where it belongs, namely, in the bin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- I just want you to respond to that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, let me. You would like me to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, of course this is an opening. In due course, no doubt, there will be litigation about whether or not the document should be admitted. It's a slightly puzzling position on the part of the Defence because my understanding is that in the original trial there was no dispute as to the authenticity or admissibility of the book initially until my learned friends took objection to it at some later point in the course of the proceedings --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply wrong I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: But in any event, Your Honours, we can litigate this in due course when it comes to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just make a general comment. I find the opening to verge on testifying and introducing exhibits which are not marked as exhibits yet but which are documents that make an impression in the mind of the Chamber. And to the extent that at this point there is now a dispute about the authenticity and the provenance, the relevance of the book that you are about to refer to, the Chamber feels constrained to apply the rules of admissibility before it allows you to continue talking about that. You've got to authentic it. You've got to bring in a witness to say he's the author of the book. All the requirements for admissibility. Because we -- the Chamber cannot accept that we hear what you are going to say only to throw the book out later. The book might be out, but the mind -- it's still in the mind. And the purpose for admissibility is to make sure that the mind of the Chamber is not coloured by what might turn out to be inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding is that in this Tribunal often the practice has been for documents and for material which is on the 65 ter list to be referred to during the course of the opening because Your Honours of course are professional Judges that are able -- well able to take away from your minds such things that may or may not in due course be ruled to be admissible. And for that reason, these documents and documents like it are normally permitted to be opened during the course of the opening and in due course if there are any other matters which need to be removed, then they are removed at the stage at which the evidence is litigated. Your Honours, much of the evidence in this case is hotly contested. There are a large number of outstanding applications relating to admissibility of evidence at a very early stage in the proceedings, and none of those have yet been decided. So, Your Honours, my submission is that Your Honours should hear the opening. It may assist Your Honours to determine admissibility in any event to hear what the relevance and the contexts of the documents are and then to -- in any event, to adjudicate in due course. Because we say that the material that I'm putting before Your Honours is highly relevant and that the authenticity of the document can be established and we can litigate whether or not it was admitted at the last trial. But my recollection is it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. It's really worrying when the Prosecutor stands up to make an opening submission in which according to this document he has no less than five separate extracts of this book and he doesn't even know, despite the fact that we've pleaded it in our opening brief, that this document was excluded on grounds of having no probative weight. That is a staggering state of affairs, frankly, from a man opening a case for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just make a few comments. First of all, I just want to say I accept that the Chamber is composed of professional Judges who are able to disabuse their minds of things that are irrelevant. However, it is also constituted of human beings, and you will realise that in the guide-lines that have been given, the whole question of MFI-ing documents is being forbidden precisely for that reason. If you are going to get one document you may be able to disabuse our minds of its contents. If we are going to get 150, it becomes pretty difficult, humanly impossible to do so, and therefore this Chamber intends to keep to a very bare minimum any documents that come in which may later have to be thrown out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I finish my comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Forgive me, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to reiterate what the Chamber mentioned yesterday, this is a new trial, and anything that has to be proved here has to be proved here. The arguments that things were proved in the previous trial do not make any sense at all and reference to the fact that things were thrown out, therefore they must be thrown out here doesn't make any sense. I would like -- will you please let me finish, Mr. Emmerson? Anything that is objectionable must be objected to here and the ruling will be made here, and the ruling of this Chamber is not going to be dependent on whether the ruling of the previous Chamber was consistent with our ruling. I just want to make that quite clear to all the parties right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have, I hope, A, entirely understood that, and B --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't behave like you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, can I just be absolutely clear on what we do understand the position to be. The ruling of the Appeals Chamber indicates that whilst the Prosecution is not precluded from seeking the admission of evidence that was excluded in the previous trial, the fact that it was excluded in the previous trial will be a material consideration for the new re-trial Chamber in determining whether its admission is justified according to different standards of relevance. That is the test that the Appeals Chamber laid down in its most recent ruling. It therefore cannot simply be said that the previous trial rulings are irrelevant. What is most troubling is that there is a basic minimum of professional duty on Prosecution counsel to acquaint themselves with what is the factual position on the document they are seeking to rely upon. I am assuming that Mr. Rogers did not intentionally intend to mislead the Trial Chamber, but there can be no question but that he is aware, because it says so in our opening brief, A, that objection is taken to the admission of this document, and B, that it was excluded by the previous Trial Chamber on the grounds it was probatively rubbish, if I can paraphrase your -- provide Your Honours with the ruling. Your Honours will want to consider that ruling in accordance with the Appeals Chamber judgement to determine whether the Prosecution has laid down some different evidential foundation justifying a different approach because otherwise we'd have two Trial Chambers reaching opposite conclusions on precisely the same legal and factual material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that happens every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it can happen, but no Trial Chamber would want to do that without first acquainting itself, as the Appeals Chamber indicated, with the course of the proceedings before. But be that as it may, for Mr. Rogers to stand up and put it forward to Your Honours on the basis, A, that there was no objection in the previous trial, and B, that the mattered document was not excluded, it indicates at best a significant lapse of professional standards and leads me to a more general concern. Your Honours will see in this bundle at page 22 another map hand-drawn. This map, this is the bundle of exhibits that the Prosecution proposes to put before you in opening. This map was drawn by Shefqet Kabashi as a part of his witness statement. Now, that witness is due to testify tomorrow, and as Mr. Rogers well knows there are very serious reasons to doubt whether he will in fact do so. So for him to seek to introduce before Your Honours as though it were evidence what is in effect part of the statement of a witness who he knows he may be unable to call --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Emmerson. This is not the time for the Defence to argue its case or to make --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are on an objection of one book and I'm not looking at that map you have just shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are on the objection of the book that Mr. Rogers is about to talk about, about which you stood up to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just give me a chance. You stood up, I was -- I said to Mr. Rogers can I make a few remarks, and you stood up before I made my last remark, which was going to be a repetition of what I had said a little earlier to Mr. Rogers, and I think what you are doing, you are going over and over again same issue using different exhibits. If you can just listen to what I'm saying and let me -- let the Chamber make a ruling on what Mr. Rogers is about to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Rogers, I remind you the last comment I wanted to make, I think it is important, therefore, where there is a dispute between the parties about the admissibility of a document that it be admitted in the normal course. I do not agree with you that the Chamber can read the document to determine its admissibility. Admissibility is determined before the document is tendered, and only on -- on being admitted may it be published to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that, but it's quite normal to put before the Court, I believe, documents that the Prosecution intends to rely upon during the course of the trial as part of the Prosecution's opening, and often there is contests about the admissibility of those documents and the weight or whatever that may be attached to them. Your Honours, I must take up Mr. Emmerson because he's made a number of very serious allegations against me personally. Your Honours, I entirely agree with him that it is incumbent upon counsel to check their facts, and I did check my facts, and I have in front of me an e-mail sent by Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Dixon on the 9th of January, 2007, in the course of the last trial dealing specifically with the book that I am referring Your Honours to in which they state it is admitted by the Defence for Ramush Haradinaj that the book entitled "Story of War and Freedom" from which I am quoting was compiled from a series of interviews with Mr. Haradinaj by Bardh Hamzaj. There is no dispute as to the authenticity or admissibility of the book in its entirety. How or why the Trial Chamber failed to admit it in the last occasion I don't know, but they did and they took their own decision for their own reasons but that's my understanding [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, for the sake of the record that is simply wrong. There was no agreed fact to that effect, and if Mr. Rogers --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I agree it was excluded. Your Honours should hear what it has to say, especially in the light of the fact there appears to be no objection to authenticity. Whatever the arguments may have been that were taken up last time around, I'm surprised my learned friend is reverting to arguing that it should not be admitted, given the clear statement that it's not -- that it's authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I just want to say this to you, Mr. Rogers, the Chamber is not saying you may not tender that document. The Chamber is saying you got to tender it and prove its admissibility before you tender it. The only difference is that you want us to hear it now before it's an exhibit. That's my problem. And you are welcome to say you will be tendering a document, a book, that is going to tell us what you think you -- the Trial Chamber should know about Mr. Haradinaj, but not try to tender it now when you don't have [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- in which case. Your Honours, in that case I will deal with it like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In deference to Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that the colloquy that you just had with Mr. Rogers takes care of my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was going to suggest we are dealing with opening statements and not with arguments about the admissibility of evidence at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I deal with it like this. During the course of the trial the Prosecution will produce to you a document in which the Prosecution says the accused Ramush Haradinaj indicated that he was the -- one of the first persons in the Dukagjin group along with Lahi Brahimaj, his uncle. And that together he and Lahi and his other relatives, they established the 1st Dukagjini group of the KLA. He also speaks, we say, of his return to Kosovo from Albania and in -- the Prosecution suggests that when he first returned he went to Jabllanice where he spent days checking equipment and that he accepted individuals into the organisation of the KLA, and those people included Lahi Brahimaj, Shkelzen Haradinaj, and Luan Haradinaj. There was then a period of time when he continued his activities outside of Kosovo between 1994 and 1998 and then returned to Kosovo to where, we suggest, he had created the first base and the base he had assisted in developing in Jabllanice. And he developed his network, a document we suggest says that he helped create the network in the Dukagjin area, and worked in close co-operation with his brother Daut, Shkelzen Haradinaj, and Lahi Brahimaj, also known as Maxhup. Your Honours, when the Haradinaj family compound in Gllogjan was attacked on the 24th of March, 1998, by Serb forces, Mr. Haradinaj was seriously injured. Indeed, soldiers from Jabllanice were sent to Gllogjan to help repel the attacks, but it was in Jabllanice that he and others sought refuge. It was in Lahi Brahimaj's home, away from the confrontation lines, in the relative safety of Jabllanice that he recovered from his injuries. Inevitably, as the armed conflict progressed, we say, the nature of the close co-operation between the two headquarters and the family network changed. Rrustem Tetaj, a former career JNA artillery officer and KLA commander will describe the changing nature of the command structure of the KLA. He will recall going to Gllogjan in April 1998, shortly after the Serb attack on the Haradinaj family compound, which was in March 1998, in order to join the KLA. There he was introduced by KLA soldiers in Gllogjan to Ramush Haradinaj as the commander. And at this meeting with Ramush Haradinaj, also present with him was Idriz Balaj, introduced by Mr. Haradinaj to Mr. Tetaj as Togeri or Toger, whom Ramush Haradinaj described as a person experienced in warfare. Your Honours, Mr. Tetaj will say that he was accepted as a KLA member and commander in the immediate area of the Gllogjan headquarters. And he describes, together with another KLA commander, Shemsedin Cekaj, the organisation of the KLA moving from village-based commands who were co-operating together, to a more formal subzone structure under the authority of subzone commanders. This occurred towards the end of May 1998 at a meeting organised by Ramush Haradinaj, where both Mr. Tetaj and Mr. Cekaj became subzone commanders, as did Ramush Haradinaj himself. Another subzone commander will give evidence that village commanders reported to the subzone commanders and that Ramush Haradinaj would be in charge of the zones. What is clear is that Ramush Haradinaj was seen at this time as a person with significant influence in the area and one to whom great respect was owed within the Albanian culture. Shemsedin Cekaj preferred in the last trial to adopt Mr. Emmerson's suggestion when cross-examined that it was Ramush Haradinaj that was trying to organise things in that area and that the relationship at this time was that of Ramush Haradinaj being first among equals. Cekaj stated in the course of evidence that "Ramush Haradinaj was someone who was very important and enjoyed great respect." Your Honours, can I show you now, please, a map showing the division of the subzones in May 1998. It's a map that was drawn by Mr. Tetaj in the last trial, and he explained - just give me a moment to turn it up in the book - it's page 9 in the map book. Your Honour, we can in due course produce larger versions of this to make it a little bit more clearer, but if Your Honours look to the left of the map and in the area where you now know the Gllogjan headquarters to be, you will see that he has drawn on the map a subdivision of that area, and you can see that they marked 1, 2, 3, and 4. Starting at the bottom, it's a little unclear but there is a number 1 in the middle of the circle. You can see the slightly hatched area to the right, and then if you just come into the centre of the circle you can actually see a number one. Above that is 2, 3, and 4. Now, he explained, Mr. Tetaj, that it was agreed that Ramush Haradinaj would become the commander of subzone 1, that he, Tetaj, would be the commander of subzone 3; and that Shemsedin Cekaj would be the commander of subzone 2. Your Honours, it perhaps doesn't matter at this stage who the commander of subzone 4 was, but you can see it was divided in May of 1998 into this area. And Your Honours, this subzone organisation continued through May 1998. And we say that Ramush Haradinaj, and the evidence will show by looking at minutes of various meetings that were held, and the testimony of witnesses that spoke about this, that Mr. Haradinaj recognised that whilst he had established formal control of the subzones around Gllogjan, the family ties with the Jabllanice headquarters were no longer sufficient for the efficient operation of the whole zone, thus requiring the establishment of a formal structure to control the whole area. And, Your Honours, we submit that in evidence that we hope will be admitted in due course in relation to what Mr. Haradinaj himself may have said about this, that the -- by the 23rd of June he had managed to establish control of the subzones and consolidated them to the point where he was able to unify KLA headquarters. And that that had occurred by the 23rd of June and from the 23rd of May 1998. And as that developed, he then began to oversee in a more authoritative manner the activity of the Jabllanice headquarters itself to balance it between Jabllanice and Gllogjan. So essentially, midway through this indictment period Mr. Haradinaj, the Prosecution says and evidence will show, that he had consolidated by the end of the indictment period complete control of the two areas of the Jabllanice and Gllogjan and that transisted over the course of the indictment period. By the middle of the indictment, and particularly with the counts, by the middle of that period he had consolidated control over both. And he describes in a -- well, there's a minute at least of a meeting in which he is recorded as saying -- this is a meeting on the 23rd of June, 1998, in Jabllanice. It's on Your Honours' screen now. Obviously we haven't put all of the minute there. We've just taken the relatively parts, we say. It's the 23rd of June, 1998, in Jabllanice. We've just put the top section so you can see who it's said were present. This is in e-court 00141 at page 2. So you can see who was present and that's translated. And then there's a handwritten part which starts "Ramush Haradinaj" and the translation shows underneath that at this meeting he was saying: "In order to help one another in future we have to supply the entire people with weapons, 16 years old and above." And then this: "Other things, we need to be positioned well, organised. Friendly and family connections are not enough. I can help as a friend or a relative, but I cannot make someone else do the same." And then there's a reference to territory which I needn't trouble Your Honours with. It's there for completeness. Your Honours, we say this shows that there was a transition and a recognition on his part that there was a need for formal organisation to move away from what were family connections, family ties, and a more loose organisation to something that needed to function better and that this occurred on the 23rd of June, 1998. Your Honours, now turning to speak a little bit more about the accused themselves. Your Honours, I've already indicated that Mr. Haradinaj was, we say, one of the founder members of the KLA resistance movement together with his uncle and that, as a result of the fire-fight that took place -- and witnesses will say that as a result of that fire-fight that took place at his family compound, that his reputation within the area grew. They describe how KLA soldiers and the population in general regarded Ramush Haradinaj's actions as heroic acts of defiance effectively and came to revere him as a commander of the zone. As one KLA member Witness Hasanaj described it: "God in heaven, Ramush on earth." As he continued his organisation of the area and consolidated his control on the 26th of May, 1998, Mr. Haradinaj became leader first of all of the Gllogjan regional staff encompassing the subzones already described and in that capacity exercised authority over military and civilian matters. Gradually he expanded and then established more formal control on the 23rd of June, when at a meeting with the Jabllanice staff, and the minutes will be adduced in evidence, Mr. Haradinaj was appointed - and I'm not sure that this is particularly in dispute but my learned friends will indicate later - was appointed as commander of the operative staff of the Dukagjin Plain formalising his overall command of the Dukagjin zone, including Jabllanice and the new formations headquarters were based in Gllogjan. Lahi Brahimaj, also known as Maxhup, was the commander of the KLA's strategic stronghold in Jabllanice during the indictment period the Prosecution says. He was also a member of the KLA General Staff as finance director. It comes from a number of witnesses, including Zoran Stijovic, Petar Shala and others. At the meeting of the 23rd of June, Mr. Brahimaj briefly became the deputy to Mr. Haradinaj before he was replaced by Mr. Haradinaj some sort while later by Nazmi Brahimaj, Lahi Brahimaj's brother. Idriz Balaj, also known as Toger, was initially recruited as a KLA training officer based in Jabllanice where he trained new KLA soldiers. Your Honours will hear evidence or receive evidence from Petar Shala and Zoran Stijovic about that. After the 24th of March 1998 attack on the Haradinaj compound, he transferred to Jabllanice from Gllogjan. Your Honours, we say that indicates how the headquarters were co-operating even before the 23rd of June. On the 24th of April, 1998, Mr. Haradinaj appointed Mr. Balaj as the commander of the Black Eagles, a rapid reaction unit, and that comes from a number of sources, Mr. Shala, Mr. Haskaj, Mr. Cekaj, and others. And Your Honours will recall it is he who sat with Mr. Haradinaj when Rrustem Tetaj came to offer his experience as a former JNA officer in the Yugoslav Army to develop the fighting capability of the KLA. Indeed, Mr. Balaj was often seen together with Mr. Haradinaj throughout the indictment period, and a number of witnesses will testify to that, Witness 17, 80, Kabashi, 29, Pappas, and Stijovic. It is Tetaj that speaks of Togeri, as amongst other things, a man who had a repetition for kidnapping and killing Albanian Serbs and Roma in the Dukagjin area in 1998. He also said that he had not himself witnessed these things and that many bad things were laid at the door of Togeri. In fact, he said this: "Everything bad that happened was attributed to him." It doesn't mean, Your Honours, that it wasn't done by him. I accept that. But evidence of general reputation is admissible. He confirmed, however, that Toger and his men were entering villages looking for people who were wanted and that he had seen names written in Toger's notebook, but he did not know why they were there. He confirmed that there were lists of people circulating that had been drawn up to compromise individuals. Your Honours, it's the Prosecution case that throughout the indictment period regardless of the issue of formal control that the accused worked closely together to advance the goals of the KLA in the Dukagjin area which included through the commission of crimes and at the detention facility those crimes being committed in particular at the detention facility which had been established in Jabllanice. Witnesses describe Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj together at Jabllanice at the place in which the detention facility was located, which was a property owned by a relative of Lahi Brahimaj and is central to the crimes charged in this case. Your Honours, it's the Prosecution case that these accused sought to establish KLA control of the zone, not just through an armed struggle against Serbian forces, forces that they regarded as occupying powers, but also through the brutal elimination of opposition by civilians who were or were perceived to be collaborating with Serb forces or otherwise not supporting the KLA, regardless to be whether they were Serb, Roma, Egyptian/Ashkali, or Kosovar Albanian. They thus pursued a common criminal purpose which involved commissions of crimes against persons perceived to be spies and collaborators with Serbia or Serb forces or otherwise considered not to be supporting the KLA. Members of the KLA abducted, interrogated, and mistreated those persons and often murdered them. And these acts of violence created an atmosphere of fear and intimidation within the population of the Dukagjin zone and elsewhere in Kosovo where the KLA was operating. Your Honours, within the free area described by the witnesses I have already addressed, away from the immediate confrontation lines, the KLA were able to act more openly. As Shemsedin Cekaj put it: "Along the main road, Peje to Decani to Gjakove, the villages that were close to the road were at risk, and the KLA soldiers were positioned there, in those villages, while in the internal parts they could carry out other duties, secondary duties, or be with their families. So the situation was like that, that they also carried out other duties, family duties, or other personal business." Your Honours, we say that with that greater freedom, the KLA and these accused could consolidate their control of the area through the rooting-out of opposition whether it be Serbs, Albanians, or other ethnicities, and those suspected of collaboration or treachery in any way were targeted. Indeed, from 1994 the KLA had publicly claimed responsibility for murders and other attacks against collaborators and others not supporting the KLA through its communiqués, which have been put into the evidential bundle of the 65 ter lists, and to the KLA communiqués to the Kosovar Albanian and Serb populations published in the media between 1994 and 1998. For example, on the 11th of December, 1997, the KLA introduced itself in its communiqué number 40 by announcing that it had turned "the barrel of a gun against the invader and traitors." That's -- comes within the 65 ter numbers of 00953, 00931, 00340, pages 3324 to 3325. Throughout 1998 the KLA announced and claimed responsibility for attacks and punitive measures against collaborators, and they claimed responsibility for attacks against Serbian police. On the 4th of March, 1998, the KLA General Staff publicly declared "death to enemies and traitors." That comes from Jakup Krasniqi, 00328, page 37, and elsewhere. The threatening language of the communiqués, we say, leaves no room for doubt as to what will happen to those suspected of collaborating. In its communiqué number 42, it declares that on 13th February 1990, but given the context, Your Honours, it must be 1998, Mustafe Kurti, a collaborator with the occupier, was liquidated. And immediately underneath, on 19 February, 1998, the criminal Nebojsa Cvejic, a member of the Serbian police force was liquidated at Luzhan near Podujeve. In a communiqué in December 1997, the KLA declared that on the evening of 28 November 1997, Dalip Dugolli, a collaborator and one of Milosevic's most trusted men, was killed. And in its communiqué number 39 from November 1997 the KLA declared: "The Albanian nation abhors the aggressor and its terrorism; it detests and despises traitors and betrayal that jeopardise and risk the fate of our liberation war." Your Honours, it's clear that the targeting and elimination of collaborators was threatened and encouraged from the earliest beginnings of the KLA. And it's also clear that this aim continued into 1998. In particular, the KLA issued a further communiqué, number 47, from Pristina on the 12th of May 1998, and published in Pristina in the Koha Ditore newspaper in Albanian on the 13th of May, 1998, in which the KLA declared -- Your Honours have there the document which is in e-court 00328, and then we've taken the part that we are wishing you to look at. And in there it says: "On the orders of the UCK, UCK or KLA General Staff, successive operations against invasion troops were carried out in operational zone number 1, that is the operational subzones of Drenice, Erenik, Dukagjin, Pashtrik, and Llap. In the course of bitter fighting on the front, the invading forces suffered major human and material losses. Throughout this period, operations were also carried out against Albanian collaborationists who, despite earlier warnings, did not abandon their anti-national courses of action." Your Honours, in addition, contemporaneous Serb security service and police reports - and I am conscious of what Mr. Emmerson said yesterday about those documents and the source of the content of them, but nevertheless Mr. Stijovic and other Serb police witnesses produce a large number of reports, for what they are worth, in which there are complaints of violence and intimidation by members of the KLA and against those not supporting them or deemed spies and collaborators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you? Would that be a convenient time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may have five minutes and then it will be because I'll be turning to the counts. I may not even be five minutes. Your Honours, the fact such targeting was carried out in the Dukagjin zone in July 1998 is borne out in the evidence of Witness 17. He described being given a list in July 1998 by the KLA commander of Baran valley area, Din Krasniqi, who the Prosecution says had been appointed by Ramush Haradinaj. Your Honours will get that from the evidence of Mr. Hasanaj. And on that list were a number of wanted persons, some variously described as collaborators. Amongst those on that list was Zenun Gashi who was also abducted by the KLA and whose body was later recovered, among others, at the Radoniq lake, and there will be evidence relating to his abduction and death in this case. And also on that list was Skender Kuci who is a named victim in Count 5. He was seen at Jabllanice, and there he was beaten and tortured and ultimately murdered whilst in KLA custody. Your Honours, in the context of this conflict which also involved the legal use of force, the Prosecution says these accused adopted illegal means to achieve their goal of control. Those illegal means are described in the indictment and they form the subject of the six counts which I'll be turning to very shortly, and it's through the adoption of those illegal means that the accused became part of the joint criminal enterprise. Indeed, they worked together to torture, cruelly treat, and murder those considered traitors to the KLA cause. Each of the accused shared the intent to murder, cruelly treat, and torture the victims. Haradinaj, Balaj, Brahimaj, other KLA soldiers, including other members of the Brahimaj family worked together to suppress and eliminate perceived opponents through murder, cruel treatment, and torture committed at the detention facility in the KLA barracks in Jabllanice. And, Your Honours, the crimes to which I will now turn are examples of the suppression and elimination of the perceived opposition by the KLA. And, Your Honours, that is, I hope a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll have several reminders. Your Honours, turning now to consider the individual counts on the indictment. Your Honour, Count 1 on this indictment alleges murder, cruel treatment, and torture in relation to three victims: Ivan Zaric, a Serb; Burim Betja; and Agron Berisha, two Roma/Egyptian. Your Honours, witnesses will, in dealing with this count, will say that as part of the conflict, the armed conflict, around 19th of May, 1998, Serbian forces attacked the village of Grabanice - and Your Honours will recall I mentioned this village will have some significance, and this is the first place in which it does - in the municipality of Kline. Your Honours, witnesses describe the nature of that attack. They say that there was two days of shelling, albeit less on the second day, followed by a full-scale ground attack. But despite that attack and despite the armed conflict, those living in that area still had to try to survive and the essentials of life had to carry on. Your Honours, at the time of the attack around the 19th of May, 1998, three young men or boys, the three victims, went from their village of Dollc, which is about 10 kilometres from Grabanice, to mill their corn to flour at the Grabanice mill. According to Witnesses 31 and 66, the young men went together to mill their grain on a horse-drawn cart. One was Ivan Zaric and the other two were the Roma that I mentioned. They came from a small community where Serb, Roma, and Catholic Albanians lived in harmony together. Normally this journey would take a couple of hours, but these three young men/boys never returned. Witness 80 describes seeing them that day at the mill at Grabanice. He says that there were two Albanian -- who he calls children aged between 16 and 17 on a cart that came to the mill. And third person remained outside on the horse. The two Albanian children, he says, were related and from the village of Dollc. He said they were polite. He describes seeing them being taken from the mill by two members of the KLA, Hazir Morina and Shaqir Krasniqi, and they were taken to a house in Grabanice nearby where those two men beat the boys with sticks. The two men then declared that they were taking them to Jabllanice. A few days or so later Witness 80 describes seeing them again, this time what he refers to as a prison in Jabllanice. By this time he himself had been detained and was working in the kitchen of that prison area in a barracks or a type of headquarters. He locates that place on the left-hand side of the road from Zhabel. Your Honours may recall that Zhabel is to the south of Jabllanice, and he says it was near a mosque and cemetery and what he describes as an ambulance station. Your Honours, I'm going to show you now a series of photographs of the village of Jabllanice and the location of where the Prosecution says witnesses will identify the prison or barracks building and some of the pictures of the buildings themselves. A number of these have already been shown to witnesses in the last trial and identified particularly by Witness 3 and Witness 6 as the place where they were detained in Jabllanice. And Your Honours, perhaps I can just take you through this small slide show. My learned friends have got copies of these as well. Your Honour, the first slide is page 13 of your map bundle. This is an aerial photograph looking at the village of Jabllanice and you can see the main road running through Jabllanice, and the view in this photograph is looking essentially from the direction of Catholic Gllogjan towards where Zhabel would be. And if you follow the road starting in the bottom right-hand corner of the photograph and follow it down into the photograph, you see the mosque on the hill and there's a little cemetery behind, and to the side you can just see some of the gravestones actually as you turn the bend in the road. And on the bend in the road you see a red brick building and some objects in front and the cemetery area there. Following around the road you can see it turning into the distance and a little group of red-tile-roof buildings. And beyond those red-tile-roofed buildings is the facility at which the Prosecution says these individuals were detained. I turn you now to the next map, photograph. This is an aerial view of the village, and if I then just turn you over straight away because this document is in e-court 03036, page 2, we've annotated the next slide just to try to orientate or help orientate around where we are. And this time you can see Catholic Gllogjan is to the north and Zhabel to the south, and the place at which we say these individuals were detained is the building shown on the left-hand side of the road coming out from Zhabel as you enter the village of Jabllanice. Your Honours can see it there circled. Actually, if you imagine driving your way in on that road as you come up and you come around the bend where the wooded area is, that's the area of the point of the two meeting roads where the mosque is. You can imagine looking at it from both directions, just to help orientate a little bit about the geography of this particular area. Turning the page, there's the first photograph of the building, and actually if you do a comparison, I don't know, maybe you can from the physical documents, you can see in 15 the shape of the building outlined, the one that's circled, and then you can sort of pick it up a little bit from this photograph, 16, e-court page 2 in 03037, and you can see the road going into Jabllanice. This is map page 16, photograph that's being shown. And a walled area, red-tiled building to the left. And if you look along the wall going into the photograph you can see what appears to be a ruined sort of gate which appears it had a top on it at some point. If I can turn the page to the next slide, 03037, e-court page 3, you will see the gate, this time really coming from the direction of Catholic Gllogjan. And just in -- the top of the wall in the left-hand side of the photograph you can see poking above it the red tiles of the previous building. Turning to the next slide or the next page if you're looking into this book, this is in e-court at 00357, and now we have a view from inside the compound -- I'm sorry, Mr. -- I'm sorry, I didn't see you stand up.
