It's not the way it should be done in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: That wasn't the intention. If my learned friend is unhappy, we can very easily delete the word "prison." It's what the Prosecution says is the prison. It will be a matter for Your Honours to determine whether it is or is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what you allege?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I hope that Your Honours can deal with it in that way and neutralise anything that may be upsetting my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whether you call it prison or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You will determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- we will find out from how it was used?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honours will determine what you think it was in due course. We say the building on the right-hand side of this photograph is the prison, and when I come a little bit later in my presentation I'll show you some other photographs which have been identified by witnesses, saying that that is the prison. And indeed, witnesses for whom there has been a conviction. So perhaps we'll come to it when we come to it. But let me just orientate you a little bit around this photograph. You can now see looking into it, first of all, the gate coming on the right -- the left-hand side of the photograph, and then there's a -- what appears to be a long building of some sort in front of the wall, the red-bricked -- red-faced building which appears to have a number of windows in it and no roof at this time when this photograph was taken, which the Prosecution says is some -- some good while after the actual events themselves. Clearly it's a ruin and was not, we say, at the time. Then on the right-hand side of the photograph is the taller red-tile-roof building, red brick-faced. It appears to have no plaster on it which we say is the prison. It was used as a prison. Turning the page, I'm happy to say the neutral language is there which I hope would be on all of them. This is in e-court at 03037 and page 4, and that gives you another view of the building we say contained the prison. We say it has four rooms to it, two at the front, one behind the bush, and then others behind those two rooms. And if I can just draw your attention to the man in the picture, you can see him kneeling down. On the right-hand side of the building at the ground level appear to be two black holes and a man kneeling. Your Honours, we say that's the basement, cellar area, underneath this building which forms part of the witness's narrative, he'll just say some were detained. And if I take you to the next photograph, we're now moving into where the man was kneeling, and you can see there the two -- I don't know what to describe them, windows or holes, whatever they may be, two holes looking in to what appears to be a water-filled basement. If we take the next photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do we determine that it's a water-filled?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If we take the next photograph, Your Honour, 03052, e-court page 1, this is a photograph of the basement and can see it is water-filled. That's not to say it was always water-filled, but in this photograph it is and witnesses describe how at certain times of the year it filled with water, not always but sometimes. Your Honours, so having orientated you around the photographs, can I take you now to the descriptions of some of the witnesses of what happened. Witness 80, we say, describes the building shown in the photographs. He said it had -- the prison building, he said it had red tiles -- I'm sorry, the whole building had red tiles, was close to the road with a wall, and had double gates, topped by a small roof and had a yard. And he says, Witness 80, that it was there in that yard area that he saw the three victims of Count 1 again. This is -- now he'd been detained there to take you back to the narrative and he says he saw the three again there. Although, he says, they were so badly beaten that he could hardly recognise them. Your Honour, he says that the building belonged -- that place, the photographed place, belonged to a relative of Lahi Brahimaj. He says that as you entered the yard there is a building immediately on the left which had red tiles at the time and was a long covered building with only one floor. The wall close to the road, he says, was part of the building. And he said it was that area that was a kitchen or eating place. In addition to that building, he said, within the compound area was another, and that other building he says was the prison. Your Honours have seen the photographs showing what appear to be two buildings. It was, he said, square-shaped with a roof which he described had four triangles. He said it had a floor and a cellar basement. With four rooms, two at the front and two at the back, with a corridor through the middle. He says it was built with red brick, unpainted and unplastered, so that you could see the mortar between the bricks. He says that he saw who he describes as children being taken from the basement cellar area of the prison building. He saw KLA soldiers taking them from the cellar, these being, the Prosecution says, the victims. And he says that the "big fry," he refers to saw them being taken out as well. And, Your Honours, we say that the big fry he refers to are the three accused, Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj who he says was known as Togeri, and Lahi Brahimaj. He says he saw the three young men or boys being taken into the yard, and there the soldiers beat them while the three accused watched. One of the two boys spoke Albanian and was calling out to their mothers "kuku nana jeme," and crying out for help to anyone that would help them, pleading. He says they were beaten with sticks, thought that their arms were broken as they were not in a proper shape and were not being held in their normal positions. He says they were battered, broken, and abused, this is what the Prosecution anticipates he will say when I say "he says," that's our understanding of the evidence he will give, and that he was -- one of them was, as he described, peeing himself, wetting himself. All of this while the accused watched on. He said, as he refers, boys were being -- were tied to what he describes, we say, as some sort of tree or wooden pillar. They were brought out in front of the kitchen area, which he refers to as a -- like an open mensa or a canteen. They were tied to these wooden pillars with wire with their hands tied behind their backs. Their clothes were wet as though they had been detained in the basement of the prison and they were trembling. He describes Idriz Balaj and a man called Bandash beating them, torturing them, and that Mr. Haradinaj was seated in the kitchen area. Lahi Brahimaj was standing. And he describes this way, that for him, Lahi Brahimaj, this was funny. That's the description he gives. He goes on to say that Lahi Brahimaj joined in the beating. He used everything, shoes, sticks, and he refers to the children -- again, he keeps saying "children," that's just the way he describes them. He says they couldn't stop the children peeing, I'm not suggesting they were very young children, but that's his description. One was crying "mother oh mother" in Albanian. He says that during the beating Lahi Brahimaj accused the boys of being sent by the Serb army. They were found to have 100 Deutschemarks in their pockets. And he says that in order to save themselves when they were beaten they said, "Yes, the Serb soldiers gave it to them." But he, the witness, did not believe that was true. He didn't think they were the type of people the Serbs would be sending, as he put it, without a single day of education. The beating, he says, continued for about 20 minutes. He then saw Idriz Balaj take a large sharp knife from a sheathe hanging on his belt. Balaj said "I am only here to kill people." He placed the knife on the ear of one of the three and then sliced off the ear whole. The other two boys, he says, screamed. Immediately after that the beating continued and Witness 80 heard Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj, Toger, speak about giving them papers to Drenica. That expression, he says, meant that they would not be seen anymore, that they would be executed. And he said after the ear cutting he couldn't watch anymore, went to the back of the building, the kitchen, area, canteen, pretending to do so something. In addition to Witness 80, the Prosecution says Witness 81 will provide evidence corroborating the account of this witness and providing his own account of what he saw. Your Honours, we recognise that there are internal differences between the accounts of the witnesses and between their own accounts, and Your Honours in due course will need to assess the weight to attach to each of their evidence should they be heard. But they are central to this count so I must open them. Your Honours, Witness 81 broadly, we say, corroborates the account of Witness 80. Witness 81 was a member of the KLA but he was not based in Jabllanice. He had been, he says, sent to the prison and there had met Nazmi Brahimaj and Lahi Brahimaj, who he knew as Maxhup. He describes, he says, the prison being located on the road to Zhabel at the end of the road out of the village of Jabllanice as you travel towards Zhabel. And, Your Honours, it clearly is. He describes the prison as being on one level with a roof and a basement, like an abandoned-type house with no windows or doors and no paint or plaster on the outside walls. There were four rooms, he says, two at the front and two at the rear. And there was a basement, he says, that was partly filled with water. He says that in the basement was seven prisoners, three young men, a Serb and two Roma, and four more elderly people, two men and two women, between -- caution with "elderly," between 40 and 60. He assumed the women, he says, were Serb because they were not wearing the typical "shamija," head-scarf, worn by Albanian women. He said the prisoners looked as though they'd been beaten and looked very thin. Later that same day, Witness 81 saw Lahi and both Ramush Haradinaj and Idriz Balaj. He had known Ramush Haradinaj since 1995 and had met him several times since March 1998. He describes the relationship between Ramush Haradinaj and Lahi Brahimaj as one where Ramush Haradinaj referred to as Lahi Brahimaj as "dajko," meaning maternal uncle. He says the Brahimaj's were based in Jabllanice and the Haradinajs in Gllogjan, but essentially they were all one big family. Sometimes that morning when he had arrived at the prison he was told to go outside by Lahi Brahimaj. He saw the two Roma and the Serb victim being taken from the basement. We say that is who he saw. There were about 12 KLA soldiers outside, including the three accused. He describes the prisoners being sworn at, interrogated, and beaten because they were considered to be Serb spies. He heard, he says, Ramush Haradinaj swearing at them and insulting them, saying things like: Where are your Serbian forces? I shall kill you and fuck your Serbian mother. He says they were interrogated in Albanian but mainly by Lahi Brahimaj but also by the other two accused, Togeri and Ramush Haradinaj, about the whereabouts of Serb forces. Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj were swearing but they were mainly beating them. Lahi Brahimaj, he says, used a baseball bat. Nazmi Brahimaj and Ramush Haradinaj also joined in the beating. Toger said, "This is how you treat the enemy." Haradinaj punched one of the Roma several times with his fist until the boy fell to the ground. And he explains that later, sometime later in 1998, Ramush Haradinaj told him that he, Ramush Haradinaj, hated Roma. The Roma boys were screaming in Albanian, "Please don't kill us. We are with you." Towards the end of the beating he saw Idriz Balaj cut off the ear of the Serb boy with a knife. Lahi Brahimaj then hit the boy on the head with a baseball bat causing one eye to bleed heavily. He says Idriz Balaj grabbed the Serb boy by his hair on the back of his head and took out the bleeding eye with his knife. He then turned to the two Roma and stabbed them several times to the chest area. Witness 81, he says, heard Ramush Haradinaj and Idriz Balaj say to the soldiers present "take them to Drenica," this was, he says, an expression learnt in the KLA to mean liquidate or execute prisoners, in particular Serbs, but also Albanians and Roma considered collaborators. He says the reason the phrase was taught was to avoid prisoners panicking if they were to learn of their fate. Ramush Haradinaj then said to him, Witness 81, and others standing by, "Take them to Drenica to Father Adem." A reference to Adem Jashari, a KLA commander killed in an attack by Serb forces and regarded as one of the KLA's first martyrs. Although Witness 81 was from a different command, he acted out of respect for Ramush Haradinaj. He took the prisoners he had come for out of the compound together with other local KLA members. They were taken to the ambulance station first but they did not leave there alive. Their bodies were later dumped by local KLA. Your Honours, turning to Count 2 -- and I can say, Your Honours, that the bodies of these three victims have not been recovered. Turning to Count 2, this is a count relating to murder, cruel treatment, and torture, and the victims of this count are Uke Rexhepaj and Nesret Alijaj, two Roma/Egyptian men. Witnesses 54, 78, and 79 provide evidence that on the 20th of May 1998, at around the same time as the events in Count 1 and the Serb attack on Grabanice, two Ashkali/Roma/Egyptian civilians, Uke Rexhepaj and Nesret Alijaj, who were related, were abducted while cycling on the road between Grabanice and Dollovo to feed their cattle. Their family has never seen them again. Although in 2003 Uke Rexhepaj's clothing was later identified among artefacts being displayed by the ICRC for the purpose of identifying those missing from Kosovo. Witness 54 said that they were abducted by armed soldiers and taken away in a car. They were taken to Jabllanice where they were seen by Witness Kabashi, a member of the KLA, the Prosecution says, based in Jabllanice since 9 April 1998. He describes them as two men of Roma ethnicity who were related, father-in-law, he says, and son-in-law. He had seen them earlier that morning in Grabanice being detained by KLA soldiers with others at a Serb house. He says they were being accused of being Serb collaborators. He says that at Jabllanice their hands were tied behind their backs with wires, he saw them in the prison at Jabllanice, and they were being kept there for only one day. He spoke with Brahimaj, Lahi Brahimaj, about the prisoners, and he describes Lahi Brahimaj as the main commander of the KLA hierarchy in Jabllanice, together with Alush Agushi. Lahi Brahimaj told him they were being sent to Drenica and he confirms, like both Witnesses 80 and 81, that that meant they were to be executed. The Prosecution says that both these victims were murdered whilst in the custody of the KLA. The prison Kabashi describes being in a house used as a barracks belonging to the relatives of Lahi Brahimaj and located on the road to Zhabel on the outskirts of Jabllanice village, about 500 metres from Lahi Brahimaj's own home. And he drew a sketch to show where the prison and barracks were located. Your Honours, that is the sketch Mr. Emmerson has already referred to, but in our submission it shows largely what is already clear from the photographs and from the aerial photographs and the witness -- evidence of others where the location of this place was. And Your Honours can see, shown I think on the screen, that the map that he -- sketch map that he drew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to have to object for the same reasons as before. This is part of his witness statement. It's not right for the Prosecution to seek to admit it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It's part of his evidence that the Prosecution expects he will give. He's here and I hope that Your Honours can just look at it now and deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The Chamber did make its remarks a little earlier before the break about tendering documents, exhibits without witnesses. And it's all very well to say you will show a sketch to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'll leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, he, Kabashi, explains that he had seen other prisoners detained there from when he first went in early April 1998, and two men, Afrim Morina and another Idriz, he didn't know his other name, being detained as spies, and Lahi Brahimaj kicking one or other of them. In addition he describes other beatings and torture for other individuals, in particular one Roma from Budisalc village near Kline, who he describes being severely beaten and cut with a bayonet and so badly injured that he died. As far as Kabashi himself could ascertain, his only crime was to have been carrying a camera while travelling from Budisalc to Kralan. The victim saying the camera was for his pictures of his marriage, but he was being beaten on suspicion of taking pictures of KLA positions. Your Honours, turning to Counts 3, 4, and 5. Your Honour, I intend to deal with these together because the evidence of the witnesses is so overlapping, to try to separate them out is very problematic, so I hope Your Honours will forgive me for taking them together. Again, they involve murder, cruel treatment, and torture. Count 3, the victim is a -- a Witness 6, a Catholic Kosovar Albanian. Count 4, the victims are Nenad Remistar, a Serb traffic police officer, a Bosnian man whose name is unknown, who worked for the Serb power company Elektrokosova, and three Montenegrins whose names are not known. And Count 5 the victims are Witness 3, a Kosovar Albanian; a man called Pal Krasniqi, a Catholic Kosovar Albanian; and Skender Kuci, a Kosovar Albanian. Your Honours, amongst the victims that Shefqet Kabashi mentioned was a man who he said will have been abducted between Kline and Gjakove. This man, he said, had a Mercedes car which was taken by the KLA commanders at Jabllanice. Kabashi gives his first name and place of birth which is the same as that of Witness 6 and describes this man as being badly beaten. Witness 6 is a Catholic Albanian civilian who was abducted on Friday, the 13th of June, 1998, whilst he and his family were driving in his Mercedes Benz 200 vehicle along the Gjakove-Kline road. He left home about 11.30 that morning to go to Kline. He and his family had passed through Grabanice and been turned back at the entrance to Dollovo by Serb soldiers. But on the way back to Gjakove he was stopped again along the main road at a place between Gjakove and Kline by approximately ten KLA soldiers wearing a mix of camouflage and civilian clothes. His car was searched. He was detained at the roadside for about two hours with his family. He had a pistol on him which was seized together with all documents. This is the evidence that he gave. He says he had a licence for the pistol but it was a police-issued weapon, and issued to reserve police. It had in fact been his father's. He also had on his person a photograph of himself with a retired Albanian policeman in police uniform. After about two hours of his detention of his detention at the side of the road, another car came along the road. The soldiers fired some shots and then brought the car to near where he was. It was a light blue Opel Kadett with Gjakove licence plates beginning DJ. Soldiers asked if he recognised the car, but he said he didn't. Shortly after this, about 20 minutes later, Witness 6 and his family were taken in the two vehicles, the Kadett and the Mercedes, towards Jabllanice. He was in the Kadett with his wife, and a soldier and the children were in the Mercedes. Inside the Kadett he saw some photographs. They were of a policeman who worked in Gjakove whom he knew as Nenad. Nenad was from the Binxh village in Kline municipality and worked in Gjakove. Witness 6 believed Nenad was a Serb or a Montenegrin who worked as a policeman. Your Honours, this man, this Nenad, the Prosecution says is Nenad Remistar. He was the owner of a light blue Opel Kadett, was a Serbian traffic police officer, and he is the victim of Count 4 in this indictment. It's our case that he was abducted at the time the Kadett was stopped on the road on 13th of June 1998. He left his home travelling to work at about half past 1.00 in the afternoon. He had gone in the blue Kadett, and he is described as having short light brown to blond hair - there is significance of this - blue eyes and clean-shaven. He never returned home from his trip to work that day, has never been heard from or seen since. His body has not been recovered. Returning to Witness 6, on the way to Jabllanice, now travelling, they stopped in a convoy stopped in Neople village where his wife and children were told to get out. He wasn't allowed to leave and they travelled on to Jabllanice. They arrived at Jabllanice and he was taken into the compound, to a room close to the entrance of the compound of the building the Prosecution describes as the prison. He says he was initially taken to a single-storey house with red bricks and four rooms in the middle of the courtyard, and he identified this photograph, showing I hope now, as the four-room house. Your Honours can see it's the same photographs -- part at least of the same photographs you have been looking at and the man kneeling in the corner there. He went on to describe the basement and said there was water in the basement, and he was held in the building for six weeks, being released on the 25th of July, 1998. Once he was taken into the building he was placed in one of the rooms and beaten by soldiers until he describes them being exhausted. He says one after the other, sometimes with a baseball bat, sometimes with other things, whatever they could lay their hands on, is part of his testimony. During the six weeks he was there he was beaten often. One of the beaters was Lahi Brahimaj, known as Maxhup, the others were Nazmi Brahimaj, Lahi's brother, and his cousin Hamza. They were the initiators of the beatings. But on the first day and night of his detention, he was kept in a building different from the four-room building. He was kept there with a man called Nenad he had seen in the photographs in the car, and he drew on a photograph, which I think is being shown now, in the last trial the room in which he was initially kept that first night, photograph 65 ter 00333. And Your Honours can see it's in the long building as the entrance to the compound. It was here, he says, that Nazmi Brahimaj beat him until he, the victim, lost consciousness. He was beaten with a baseball bat on his legs and his arms. He was tied with rope to Nenad in the same room. They were both beaten. He said, "We stayed there all night and we were beaten and tortured and we had lost consciousness, me and Nenad." Nazmi and a group of soldiers took turns to beat them, Nazmi Brahimaj. He was with Nenad, he says, for 24 hours and then Nenad was taken away by two soldiers. When he was taken away, he, Nenad, wasn't able to walk. He said they both had, he and Nenad, the same injuries. They were both moved after the first night to the four-room building. Witness 6 was kept in the room on the left side of the building as you enter. He was not kept with Nenad. He didn't see him again and didn't know what happened to him. The Prosecution says the account of what happened to Nenad Remistar is picked up by Witness 81. I'll return to Witness 6. Still with Nenad Remistar. Witness 81 describes returning to Jabllanice about three weeks after the ear-cutting incident. This would appear to fit, the Prosecution says, with the abduction of Nenad Remistar on the 13th of June, 1998. He describes, Witness 81, being sent to the prison at Jabllanice in order to take two Roma and an Albanian prisoner to Novoselle where there was another KLA prison. He had an order to take to Lahi Brahimaj which he delivered. He saw the three prisoners who he had to take and said they were not too badly beaten. He said there were a total of 15 prisoners and was present when Lahi Brahimaj interrogated and beat a policeman called Nenad who had blond, fair hair. He was questioned about patrols and check-points. His hands were tied behind his back and he was beaten by Lahi Brahimaj all over his body with a baseball bat. He was already hardly able to stand, he says, before this interrogation. Witness 81 took his three prisoners away to Novoselle, returned to Jabllanice the next day, he had gone to take three prisoners to another place and had become somehow involved with the interrogation of this witness -- this victim. He returned the next day to discover that this victim, Nenad Remistar, and two other Serb policemen he said who were also detained in the basement, and all the other prisoners, had gone. He did not ask Maxhup -- the prisoners in the basement had gone. He didn't ask them what had happened but understood, he says, they had all been killed. Doesn't explain any more about that. Returning to Witness 6, he wasn't kept in the basement, he was kept in the rooms. He said for the first four weeks he was kept locked in the room on the left-hand side of the building and saw no one other than those that came, he says, to torture him. He couldn't tell day from night because he was locked in the room and beaten, wasn't allowed out, and the window was barred with wooden planks. He was given a piece of bread and marmalade, a little to drink, filthy water in glass jars, he was sick and he was often unconscious. They took his watch and he was almost naked. He couldn't count the assailants because they were numerous. This is his evidence. For the second two weeks he had more freedom to move and had better food and was able to eat bread and beans. And after about two weeks of his detention, they brought four other prisoners, he said, a Bosnian and three Montenegrins. Your Honours, it's fair to say that this witness is a little unclear about precisely the periods of time between the six weeks for how long he was kept, whether it was two or four weeks before he was allowed a little bit more freedom, but Your Honours will no doubt be able to deal with that when you read and understand his testimony. But essentially he gives an account of increasing amounts of freedom. And then describing -- during this detention period, these four other prisoner, a Bosnian and three Montenegrins -- the other victims in Count 4. The Bosnian was a Muslim working in Decan in the Elektrokosova company. The four were together with Witness 6, the four new people -- the Bosnian and three Montenegrins were with Witness 6 for about three days he says. He describes how the four men were beaten during the three days that they were there. They were beaten with baseball bats, they were stabbed with knives, their clothes were covered in blood. He describes the victims being pricked with knives all over their bodies, about 1 centimetre deep, three of them. They were bleeding and because of the beating they spat blood. They were covered in blood. That's his testimony. There was blood on the floor. He says that during the beatings Nazmi Brahimaj and Hamza were there. On about 10.00 in the evening on the third day the four men were taken away. He never saw them again. During the beating of the man from Elektrokosova, the soldiers were telling him, you are working for Serbia, you are working for Elektrokosova, and you are interrupting the power-supply, all the time the KLA soldiers were beating him. Throughout the time he was detained there, Witness 6 saw Lahi Brahimaj continuously, regularly. Asked what this meant, he said, "Well, two days would not pass without seeing Lahi Brahimaj ..." That was his testimony. He went on to describe the three, three men, coming to beat him regularly with baseball bats and fists. He said, "For two weeks, I didn't know where my face was, where my neck was. I was all swollen up because of the beatings." They also sent others to beat him. All three, Lahi Brahimaj, Nazmi Brahimaj, and Hamza Brahimaj weren't there all together at the same time. When asked about his conditions of detention he said, "During my stay for the first three weeks there was nothing in the room, only the floor. No covering, no blankets, nothing." About two weeks before he was released he had a little bit more freedom. It appears he could move around, this time in the village a little. Three other people were brought in at that time. One was an Albanian man from Zahaq brought in the boot of a car in a metallic Mercedes and he was beaten, the Prosecution says, and tortured until he died. When he arrived, the man in the car, they took him from the trunk of the car and beat him, they being Nazmi Brahimaj, Lahi Brahimaj, and others. He says he was ultimately sent for treatment -- the man was ultimately sent for treatment, but he died. That man was kept in a room different from Witness 6 and was beaten by Nazmi and Hamza. The Prosecution says that man, the man in the Mercedes from Zahaq was Skender Kuci, the victim in Count 5. Later again they brought two other prisoners. One was Pal Krasniqi, another victim in Count 5. He was wearing sports clothes, a blue track suit, and Witness 6 was shown a photograph of Pal Krasniqi and was able to identify the man as one of the men who was brought in. He says Pal Krasniqi was a Catholic. The other man who came a few hours after Pal Krasniqi is, the Prosecution says, Witness 3, another victim of Count 5. These two men, Pal Krasniqi, Witness 3, and Skender Kuci were put together in one room. He, Witness 6, says he saw Pal Krasniqi and the other man, Skender Kuci, being beaten with a baseball bat, and describes them being in a horrifying state. He didn't see Witness 3 being beaten. Pal Krasniqi and the other man, Skender Kuci, were beaten continuously on the second day of their detention. Witness 6 goes on to describe how the three, he says, tried to escape. He says Witness 3 was able to get away but the other two could not. They couldn't walk fast. They were recaptured, beaten, and tortured again. Hamza Brahimaj beat them. Skender Kuci was later taken to Irzniq, but Pal Krasniqi was left in Jabllanice. In the time the other man, Skender Kuci, was there, Witness 6 describes him as lying down with his eyes closed. He said he was fat and also swollen because of the beating, so his eye -- he could not open his eyes. He was all swollen. He was fat but because of the beating he said, "I thought his clothes could not contain his body because of the swelling." That's at transcript 5337 of the last trial. Witness 6 describes Pal Krasniqi as beaten up very badly. He could not eat or drink anything. Witness 6 remembers being released on 25th of July 1998. He saw Pal Krasniqi shortly before he left Jabllanice and says this: "There was blood on him, he was spitting blood. His body was all blue and black because of the beating, swollen. He was lying down on the floor. I would bring him some water. He was in this shape for a week. Then I was released and left that place and I don't know what happened to him." He never saw him again. And he didn't know why he had been imprisoned. Your Honours, Pal Krasniqi's body was recovered from the Lake Radoniq canal by Serb investigators on or around the 8th of September 1998. It is the body labelled R9. An autopsy revealed that the cause of death was multiple gun-shot injuries to the head, trunk, and upper limbs. Witness 6 was never given any reason as to why he himself had been imprisoned, but it's clear, Your Honours, from the transcript in the last trial in answers to questions, I think, by Mr. Harvey in cross-examination that he was being beaten and when he was being beaten he was being questioned. And during the questioning he was asked whether he had stayed in the company of Serbs. He said they accused me of staying with Serbs. Asked further about that he said: Lahi and Nazmi were saying this. Lahi and Nazmi accused me of staying with Serbs. In answers to Judge Orie in the transcript he said: "That night when we arrived there, they asked such questions. Then they continued to torture me. And then they, the soldiers came and told me, you are a spy of Serbia." As a Catholic Albanian he explained he was not, he felt, considered an Albanian, he said, for them, and even now they do not consider me an Albanian. When he was released he was given some papers, stating that the staff of the subzone of Dukagjin had ordered his car and revolver be confiscated, signed by Nazmi Brahimaj as deputy commander. And in addition he had a paper saying that he, the accused, was being conditionally -- said the accused, was being conditionally released by the staff of the subzone and that if he were to repeat his "mistakes," he would be prosecuted. He said he didn't know what his mistakes were. He confirmed that Lahi Brahimaj and his brother mistreated him continuously. Indeed, the Trial Chamber found beyond a reasonable doubt that Lahi Brahimaj personally participated in the torture and cruel treatment of Witness 6 and convicted him of the crimes of torture and cruel treatment as violations of the laws or customs of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should just give notice at this point that the Defence for Lahi Brahimaj objects to the use of any reference to convictions. As Your Honour has said repeatedly, this is a trial de novo and if the issue of conviction is sought to be relied on by the Prosecution in any degree, then we wish to brief that because we believe it to be completely contrary to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had indicated to Mr. Harvey in advance of today's hearing that I intended to open his convictions and unfortunately he hadn't mentioned this to me before I did. I shan't mention it. I think it's a matter of record, in any event, that they exist, but we can deal with what the evidential value of them is or may be in due course. I take note of what he says, that there is an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for taking note, and thank you. Are you done? Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that I thought I had made it abundantly clear to Mr. Rogers that I would take this position. I am surprised that he is surprised. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I carry on. Your Honours, by the 25th of July, 1998, and after Ramush Haradinaj's appointment as commander on the 23rd of June, 1998, the Dukagjin zone had been organised with Ramush Haradinaj as the commander. Lahi Brahimaj was appointed his deputy initially, but by the 25th of July, 1998, Ramush Haradinaj had replaced him with Nazmi Brahimaj, which may go some way to explain how the papers that Witness 6 believe was signed by Nazmi Brahimaj as deputy commander. Your Honour, the witness after his -- suffered the attacks that he had says that he continues to have trouble with his left arm and with pain in his kidneys. Your Honours, I just turn to deal a little more now with Skender Kuci, Pal Krasniqi, and Witness 3. Witness 3 was a member of a political party, the LDK, which was a political party supporting Ibrahim Rugova, leader of the LDK and whose ideal had very broadly, I don't want to get into the entire political history, but very broadly had been for a "peaceful path," solution to the situation in Kosovo. Witness 3 had been a village guard in Grabanice and was at that time in position when the Serbs attacked the village, going back now into the 19th of May, 1998. On the 21st of May he had to withdraw from the village to Jabllanice, passing through Gllogjan, and on the way he met Lahi Brahimaj, who was very angry, he says, and Alush Agushi, who accused him of being a traitor for abandoning his post. In his testimony in the Limaj trial, Shefqet Kabashi described how the villagers of Grabanice had fled the shelling to Gllogjan, Catholic Gllogjan. He described how the leaders, who he said were Lahi Brahimaj and Alush Agushi, who's another KLA member and named JCE member, asked the villagers of Grabanice why they had left, why they had fled. And he then said this in his transcript: "At that time it was very difficult to leave your place." Asked what he meant by this, he said: "Because the time was very difficult and it was difficult to leave your place of course. It was better to stay there and get killed than to flee." Witness 3 stayed for about a week in Jabllanice. He moved around a bit. He stayed for about a week in Jabllanice until the 31st of May, when he went to stay in a house in Zhabel belonging to a man called Tal Zekha. Your Honours, can I just very briefly go into private session and then very quickly out again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Another man was also in Tal Zekha's house. He too had been forced to leave Grabanice on the 21st of May in the Serb attack. But KLA soldiers came for that other man and the other man was forced to leave there by KLA soldiers who kicked and beat him, witnessed by Witness 3. He was taken away with someone called Fadil Fazliu. One of the KLA members that took them was called Ujku, or Pjeter Shala was his name, also known as Ujku. He was, the Prosecution says, a member of the MP of the KLA and a member of the JCE. He wore a black uniform, was shouting abuse at the other man and Fazliu as they were taken downstairs, all the time calling them traitors. Lahi Brahimaj began looking for Witness 3, the Prosecution says, around the 30th of June, 1998. He appeared -- Lahi appeared, at Tal Zekha's house, where Witness 3 was, and asked Witness 3 to go with him to Jabllanice. The car being driven by Lahi Brahimaj was a Mercedes car that it is said belonged to Skender Kuci. Lahi took Witness 3 to what he called the staff -- what Witness 3 called the staff headquarters in Jabllanice, where there was a prison. He was shown this paragraph and identified this as the place where he had been taken. And so perhaps it's not offensive to call it Jabllanice prison on this one because this is -- the witness identified as the prison he was taken to. He said he was kept prisoner in the building on the right-hand side in the photograph consistent with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have no pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Picture. We have vision. All right. Thank you. He says he was in the building on the right-hand side of the photograph. After he was taken there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, lest silence be thought to be consent, it is still objectionable, Your Honours. I hate to interrupt, but it really is no good keeping on plugging away with labels that should never have been on photographs in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I hear, I hear what is said. Your Honours, the witness describes being detained in that building on the right-hand side where he was put into a room. Other people came in and they beat him. There were two other people there. One was called Skender Kuci. Witness 3 was beaten with baseball bats until he lost consciousness. He says he was detained two nights and three days, but was himself only beaten on the first day. He had his hands tied at night, as did the other two men. He said Nazmi Brahimaj was one of his attackers. He kicked him. The others beat Skender Kuci and the other man. They were terribly injured, the two other men. He said Skender was black on one side, the other man was swollen. Skender Kuci was crying in pain and moaning, but the other could not move. He further described the condition of the other man, that the Prosecution says is Pal Krasniqi, as follows: "He was beaten to a pulp. He was not in a position to get up, let alone walk in the courtyard. He used to pee in his pants." At one point Witness 3 describes being taken into a room next to the one he was beaten in. There he appeared before Lahi Brahimaj who accused him of supporting the Serb police. There were two women in the room as well. Lahi told them to practice on him and the women started to beat him as hard as they could with what he described as a kind of telescope on his hands. This lasted five or ten minutes. Lahi, he said, had a revolver, which he said to Witness 3 he should use to kill himself. Another man in the room told Witness 3 to admit everything. He said, "I'll cut your throat and then you will have to admit everything." Witness 3 decided that at that point it was time to run away. When he returned to the room where the other two were, he decided he was going to run away. He escaped through a side window, did not see Skender Kuci or the other man, Pal Krasniqi, again. Your Honours should have a photograph I hope -- no? Yes? I'm grateful. Which the witness marked during the course of the last trial, and he marked two rooms, one on the right he said was the room that he escaped from and is marked SK, together with Skender Kuci, and the room on the left marked L is the room he says that he went into where Lahi Brahimaj was and where he was beaten on his hands. He ran out of the building towards the Prosecution says is a brook or a stream at the end of this compound area and escaped. He says Skender Kuci followed him but he didn't make it. After his escape, sometime later, he saw Lahi Brahimaj again. Lahi took him to his -- Lahi Brahimaj's house, and there accused him that Skender Kuci had promised the witness, 3, 10.000 Deutschemarks to help him escape. Lahi slapped Witness 3 around the face, forced him into the boot of the Mercedes car, and drove him to the staff headquarters, he describes the staff headquarters. Lahi drove him around in the trunk of the car and kicked him, and at some point he stopped the car, opened the trunk, and carried out what the Prosecution would describe as a mock execution. Lahi pulled out his gun and asked -- or a gun and asked Witness 3 if he should pull the trigger. Witness 3 said yes and Lahi fired. He saw a flame and heard a click and felt some pain but realised he had not been shot. Thank you. Lahi Brahimaj shut the trunk and drove off to Gllogjan to the home of Ramush Haradinaj. Your Honours, Witness Kabashi also describes seeing Skender Kuci and Pal Krasniqi at Jabllanice in June or July 1998. In fact, around the 10th of July, 1998, Pal Krasniqi had gone to Jabllanice to join the KLA and worked for a few days before being arrested as a spy and detained in Jabllanice prison. Kuci's name had appeared on a list of wanted persons around the 12th of July, 1998, which I mentioned earlier on, the list of wanted persons. Kuci's brother had been a police officer. He was abducted, Kuci, from his home in Zahac, also the home village of Witness Kabashi and taken to the Jabllanice compound in his own Mercedes Benz car where he was detained and beaten. Kabashi saw Kuci there and spoke to him and was told that Kuci had been accused of being a spy. He spoke to Lahi Brahimaj about Kuci and Brahimaj said that he, Kuci, was a big fish, which Kabashi took to mean a Serb spy. Kabashi said it wasn't true and that Lahi informed him he believed that Kuci was working for the Serb secret service. He also, Kabashi, saw Krasniqi -- Pal Krasniqi looking very scared, somebody that he had known, Pal Krasniqi, for a long time. And Krasniqi told him that he had admitted to being a spy under torture in order to make the torture stop. He said he had gone to join the KLA in Jabllanice, but after a few days he was accused of being a spy and imprisoned. Kabashi was troubled, went home that night, and talked to his family about the condition of the two men, who urged him to try to do something to save them. But when he returned the next day Skender Kuci was in a very bad way, his belly was bloated. He asked those in the imprisoning the men what had happened, and they said that Skender and a man from Grabanice had tried to escape. It appears, Your Honours, from the evidence that KLA subzone commander Rrustem Tetaj, who had involvement in what subsequently happened with Kuci, became aware of the detention of Kuci and informed Mr. Haradinaj who together they went to Jabllanice in order to seek the immediate release of Skender Kuci. Haradinaj spoke to Nazmi Brahimaj, calling to Rrustem Tetaj, who responded that Kuci had tried to escape and had been slightly injured and that he would be released as soon as he recovered. Ramush Haradinaj ordered that he be taken to the hospital in Irzniq. He was taken to the hospital but died of his injuries. His body was buried initially near to the mosque and cemetery in Jabllanice and was ultimately exhumed and moved. An OMPF autopsy reveals records of multiple fractures to his body. Kabashi provides a little further information as to who were responsible for beatings generally. He said those who usually beat the prisoners were Lahi Brahimaj, a man called Bandash, Pjeter Shala known as Ujku; Idriz Balaj, and two others, and he describes Mr. Balaj as being the cruellest. He recounts a particular incident relating to another man called Jah Bushati. Two protected witnesses, who will corroborate, the Prosecution says, Mr. Kabashi's account, as they recount how, to some extent at least, as they account how Jah Bushati was detained at the Jabllanice prison around the spring of 1998, and so severely mistreated while in detention that he could barely walk. He like the other victims in this case was detained and mistreated by the KLA at Jabllanice on suspicion of being a Serb collaborator. Your Honours, I'm conscious of the time. I have one count left to deal with. Is this a convenient moment to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed if it's convenient to you. We will take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I turn now to deal with Count 6. Your Honour, this is a count of cruel treatment and torture. Your Honour, turning to the victim's detention at Jabllanice, he was detained by the KLA, the Prosecution says and he says, because he was a supporter of the LDK, of Ibrahim Rugova, its leader, and he did not agree with the KLA strategies and actions. In particular, he says he was ordered by the KLA to kill eight LDK supporters, an order which he refused to obey. Lahi Brahimaj, Nazmi Brahimaj, and Alush Agushi gave him a list of names of LDK members that included his own nephew, Riza. And they asked him to kill those on the list particularly because no one would suspect him. Your Honours, he fled his own home village along with other villages following the Serb attack on Grabanice on the 19th of May, 1998. The KLA, including Lahi Brahimaj, accused, he says, the men of Grabanice of being traitors because they had not defended their positions against the Serb attack. Towards the end of May -- sorry, when I say "he says," Witness 3 stated that position. Towards the end of May 1998, the victim says he was abducted from a house in Zhabel, pursuant to an order for arrest, he says, was signed by Ramush Haradinaj and which he says he saw. Pjeter Shala, also known Ujku or Wolf and Arbnor Zejneli and other KLA members were involved in this abduction during which the victim was kicked, beaten, and called a traitor. He was taken to Jabllanice, he says, where he saw other villagers, about 20, who had also been made to go there. Lahi Brahimaj was swearing at them in the yard of the compound of the building we've already identified. He was saying: If you don't go to free your village, we will kill you, kill you all, and you won't have any place in Kosovo. He describes other KLA leaders being present, such as Mr. Haradinaj, Nazmi Brahimaj, Alush Agushi, Naser Brahimaj, and Gani Brahimaj. Lahi Brahimaj, he says, asked the villagers to return to the village to send out the Serbs. Some were calling Lahi uncle so that they may be saved he says, but Lahi said: There is no uncle here for you. During that time, that period in the yard, Lahi Brahimaj introduced Ramush Haradinaj to the gathered people as the commander Ramush Haradinaj. They --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise. Can I just ask Mr. Rogers to check whether at page 69, line 1, he meant to say Witness 3 or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I did mean to say Witness 3. That's my reference to the men at Grabanice being traitors is from him, Witness 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can it be made clear that the source of the testimony being summarised is not Witness 3. The allegation that is being summarised in relation to Count 6 is not derived from Witness 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the remainder of the passage that has been cited, although Mr. Rogers has not identified the witness or victim he is referring to, is not Witness 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, no, that's right. That one piece was from Witness 3. That's why I interjected it in case Your Honours thought I was talking about this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Okay. Thank you so much. Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Does that meet the concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just returning to the story. Yes, Mr. Brahimaj introduced Ramush Haradinaj as the commander. They were seated in the kitchen or canteen area of the barracks or prison building, and the villagers were standing in the yard. He says Mr. Haradinaj warned the villagers that they could not live in Kosovo unless they first freed their village from the Serbs. The villagers themselves left after some time. And the victim, however, remained in Jabllanice for a short period before in fact he was released. He wasn't free for very long. Your Honours will of course have to dovetail the story with other parts of the story that we have given so far. The victim says that in the end of June or beginning of July 1998 four KLA soldiers stopped him on the road between Kosuriq and Catholic Gllogjan. They handcuffed him, put him in the trunk of a car, and drove him to Jabllanice. In Jabllanice the victim saw Ramush Haradinaj, Balaj, Lahi and Nazmi Brahimaj, and others, but on this occasion Lahi Brahimaj allowed him to go home, told him he had to come back whenever he, Lahi Brahimaj, called him. Sometime later between mid-July and August 1998, the victim says he was captured again and this forms the main subject of Count 6. Lahi and Nazmi Brahimaj and other KLA members abducted him in Grabanice.
