utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I'm pausing because I wouldn't want Your Honours to be under any misapprehension. I don't know whether it's necessary to go into closed session or not, but Your Honours are fully aware of the identity of the witness who's testimony is here being summarised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the relationship that that has with other parts of the opening. I simply say it because you may be left with the impression that what you are hearing is an account from multiple witness when in fact it's an account from a single witness which crosses a number of counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope I hadn't left you with that impression. If you have, I'm sure it's been fully corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't have that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in Jabllanice the victim says he saw Haradinaj, Balaj, and Alush Agushi. The victim says Haradinaj ordered the beating of him saying: So you brought him, go ahead with your job then. The victim says Lahi Brahimaj, Nazmi Brahimaj and KLA soldiers, including one named Bandash, beat the victim. The victim says he was kicked and hit with wooden sticks or baseball bats. The victim says Balaj threatened him with a pistol to his temple and said: I never beat people. I am here to kill them. The victim says it was Haradinaj that controlled his beating to the extent that he stopped and started it. The victim was hit so hard on his genitals that he fell to the ground. Haradinaj grabbed his hair, spat in his face, and called him a traitor. After being beaten, the victim was thrown into the water-filled basement in a four-room building on the compound and he was regularly beaten in the yard. Following his detention in the basement, Lahi Brahimaj interrogated the victim and ultimately discovering that he had some use and that he could cook, Brahimaj forced him to work in the kitchen in the detention facility area in Jabllanice. A few weeks later the victim finally escaped from Jabllanice during an impending Serb attack. Your Honours, in concluding my opening remarks, the Prosecution says that having considered all of the evidence in this case and having heard the submissions of all the parties, Your Honours will be left satisfied and sure - or put it another way - satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that each of the accused is guilty of the crimes alleged in this indictment. Your Honours, those are my opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers. Mr. Emmerson -- before you start, Mr. Emmerson, I see Mr. Harvey is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only on my feet for one reason and that is because it does surprise me, it's a normal thing to do in opening a case, to inform the Judges of that which I am sure you are well aware, that -- which counts are faced by which accused. And as Your Honours will recall, I hope, Mr. Brahimaj is before you only on one -- Counts 1, 2, 4, and 6. That wasn't made clear in the opening and I feel it requires underscoring at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We -- I'm sure the Chamber is aware of the indictment and have read the indictment. We are aware of the counts that Mr. Brahimaj faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's just that his name was mentioned frequently in relation to Counts 3 and 5 as well, and I just thought it was worth underscoring at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We thank you for the underscoring. Thank you so much. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a similar note, the concern that I had which I raised just a moment ago about the manner in which Prosecution are presenting the evidence emanating from a single witness, which we understand is being put forward in this way in order to ensure that there can be no tracing or cross-referencing through the indictment which might, in one way or another, undermine protective measures, but it will become very important for Your Honours to realise that so far as Mr. Haradinaj is concerned - and I shall deal with this in a little detail in a moment or two - it is a single witness in respect of each of these counts who is making the allegations that you have heard, now potentially corroborated by a further witness. And I'll deal with numbers in due course, but it's -- one can be left with the impression that there is more than one source, where in fact, as Your Honours will see, it becomes very important in due course in analysing this case, just how narrow the impugned source of this information really is. Can I indicate before I start that the submissions that I'm going to make to you now are made solely on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand that. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I take it as my starting point that this is a new trial. It is not - as Judge Moloto has emphasized more than once - to be approached as the step-child of the original child. It is in effect a fresh trial but it is one in which the Prosecution is re-hashing or seeking to re-hash old allegations on which Mr. Haradinaj was found guilty by the trial -- found not guilty by the Trial Chamber in the previous proceedings. We recognise at the outset that this Chamber is not bound by findings of fact either way returned by the previous Trial Chamber, and anything that I say now or during the course of this trial is subject to that overarching understanding. But as the Appeals Chamber has held, it doesn't follow that what occurred at the previous trial is irrelevant. Certain issues, for example, are res judicata, decided and unappealed. Others, including disputed issues of admissibility, whilst they remain open, have been subject to guidance from the Appeals Chamber that the reason they remain open is because different questions of relevance may arise. Plainly, if no different questions of relevance arise and if the Prosecution chose not to appeal a previous ruling in the previous proceedings, then it would be difficult for them to persuade you that it is not res judicata. So to that extent, the previous trial can't simply be ignored. Much will depend on the issue to which its relevance may impinge. But it will be, we say, particularly relevant in relation to the two witnesses, Shefqet Kabashi and Witness 80, who were the basis for the Prosecution's appeal that resulted in this partial re-trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: (redacted) There's no getting away from the fact that if it were not for the absence of those two witnesses from the original trial, we wouldn't be sitting here in this courtroom today. The Appeals Chamber considered that more should have been done to hear their evidence, and as a result it ordered this partial re-trial on a confined number of allegations relating to the KLA headquarters at Jabllanice, a separate stronghold outside Mr. Haradinaj's immediate area of control. Can I ask that you be shown the map on which the Prosecution relies and which is to be admitted by agreement in evidence, which is 1.000/0026. It's been shown to you already. It's page 9 in the hard copy bundle. So it says I000/0026 rather than 1.000. It looks like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Rogers opened this to you a little earlier on, and he showed you that there were numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have it as page 9 myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this was a map marked by Rrustem Tetaj, one of the subzone commanders appointed in the emergence of what was a fledgling organisation. Your Honours will have appreciated that command structures such as they were within the Kosovo Liberation Army during the indictment period were horizontal rather than vertical, that the organisation was very much a fledgling developing and emerging throughout the indictment period. And this map represents an attempt at organisation in the early stages of the indictment period on or around the 23rd of May. And as Mr. Rogers told you, the unchallenged evidence is that there were four subzones and four subzone commanders of whom Mr. Haradinaj was one, Mr. Tetaj another, and Shemsedin Cekaj a third. And you will see if you look at the areas they are marked. The important point for Your Honours to note from this map and really the key point at the outset of these proceedings is Jabllanice's location. If Your Honours look just roughly halfway down the map on the middle crease to an oval just past the right-hand side of centre, you will see Jabllanice. It's an area on the opposite side of the Dukagjin zone from the four subzones that were created on the 23rd of May. It existed wholly outside the four subzones that were created on the 23rd of May and wholly outside any area of responsibility that could on any view be attributed to Ramush Haradinaj. It is not without reason, Your Honours, that the Prosecution has never made an allegation of command responsibility in these proceedings. The reason is because there were no effective command structures in place at any time during the indictment period which would have allowed the Prosecution to invite the Court to seek to ascribe responsibility for a failure to prevent or punish the commission of crimes. So we are dealing with a very unusual case to come before this Tribunal, the case of an emerging fledgling organisation, seeking to bring together local village commands under a single unified control over a nine-month period. I say that is important because obviously at any given time it's going to be vital for Your Honours to consider what the nature of the organisation and reality on the ground was. What you know from this map, which Mr. Rogers himself urges upon you, is that at this time at least Jabllanice operated entirely independently from the four subzones that had been created by the end of May. True it is that there were attempts made thereafter to increase co-ordination between different pockets of KLA activity in western Kosovo and elsewhere, but the notion that there was a leader or leaders operating a vertical command structure is and would be misconceived and cannot and is not alleged by the Prosecution. That's a very important starting point. Your Honours may come to the conclusion, having heard the evidence, that some crimes at least were committed. You may conclude that some crimes were committed at Jabllanice, but the issue as far as Ramush Haradinaj is concerned is whether he participated, authorised, or condoned those crimes, or was party to a joint criminal enterprise that they be committed. There is no suggestion, nor could there be on the evidence, that Ramush Haradinaj ever had day-to-day operational control over Jabllanice. There is no suggestion nor could there be on the evidence that he was ever present at Jabllanice other than on particular occasions. And with the exception of two witnesses who I'm going to focus on in this opening and who Mr. Rogers knows and recognises his case against Mr. Haradinaj stands or falls on, with the exception of those two witnesses, Witnesses 80 and 81, there isn't a single witness who suggests that Ramush Haradinaj ever did anything or was even present at Jabllanice whilst anything untoward was occurring. Witness 6, who Mr. Rogers has placed emphasis on, was detained at Jabllanice for six weeks. He never saw Ramush Haradinaj once. Witness 3, again who Mr. Rogers extensively relies upon, was allegedly detained and ill-treated at Jabllanice and elsewhere, but as you heard he was eventually taken, so it is alleged, to Gllogjan; not as Mr. Rogers mistakenly suggested to Mr. Haradinaj's home, but to the KLA headquarters in Gllogjan, where he came across the commander. Gllogjan was, of course, at that point under the command of Ramush Haradinaj. The commander, faced with a man who was alleging ill-treatment by KLA officials form Jabllanice, fed him, housed him, made him safe. This is his evidence. And the following morning gave him a clear assurance that nothing untoward was ever occur to him again and nothing untoward ever did. Skender Kuci, a man you've heard something of whose remains were subsequently discovered and who died in Jabllanice -- oh, sorry, sorry, I should rephrase that, who died having been detained in Jabllanice on Prosecution's case, as Mr. Rogers adverted to in glancing terms, the evidence of Rrustem Tetaj, which is admitted by agreement, is that he who was, you've heard, was a subzone commander on the opposite side of the Dukagjin zone from Jabllanice was made aware that a man called Skender Kuci was being detained there. He took that information, he says, to Ramush Haradinaj. What was his response? Immediately with Mr. Tetaj to drive right across the zone to find out what was going on, to discuss the situation, according to Rrustem Tetaj, with Nazmi Brahimaj; and then to order that Skender Kuci be released to a military hospital where he could be properly treated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. It's been brought to the attention of the Chamber that it is probably desirable to redact lines 22, 23, 24, 25, of page 75, and line 1 of page 76 because of something that you said, Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, if it's a reference to Witness 80 and 81, it's going to be impossible to conduct this trial without those references, so I don't think it's anything more than that, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know who's suggesting it should be redacted or why, so I can't really respond. Shall we deal with it at the close of the proceedings or is it necessary to deal with it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's deal with it -- the problem is that by the close of the proceedings it will have gone out by the time if it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if somebody could point out what the concern is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours ... Your Honours, it may be better to briefly have a discussion in private session while we deal with the issue, whether we need to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time that this Tribunal or any other international criminal tribunal, has held a full re-trial following an acquittal. And it is in a number of other important respects unique as well. So before embarking on this unprecedented process, I want, if I may, just to say a little about how we got to this point. It's over six years now since Mr. Haradinaj was first indicted. At the time he was a serving prime minister in the provisional institutions of self-government established under the auspices of UNMIK, the United Nations Mission in Kosovo. He was widely regarded as an excellent political leader, one who could unite Kosovo, secure the support of the international community, and who was committed to the protection of the rights of those pockets of Serb national minorities remaining inside Kosovo's boundaries after the war. As such, he represented a potent political threat to Serbia, which was at that time uncompromisingly committed to preventing Kosovo from achieving secession and independence and uncompromisingly committed to seeking the decapitation of its political leadership. It is widely and publicly known that high-ranking Serbian officials made forceful representations to the Office of the Prosecutor seeking to have Mr. Haradinaj prosecuted. The crimes against him in the original indictment were based upon a dossier of evidence collected by the Serbian intelligence service, the RDB, itself, an organisation that was known to engage in the basest methods of evidence manipulation. Remarkable as it may seem to those outside this courtroom, the case against Mr. Haradinaj, as it was advanced by the Office of the Prosecutor at the original trial and as it is advanced here, was and is based primarily on an investigation conducted by the Serbian intelligence services themselves. It is now a matter of public record that lawyers appointed to advise Madam del Ponte told her from the outset that there was no sustainable case against Mr. Haradinaj. She had to change her legal team more than once. In the end she found a team that was prepared to draft an indictment and prosecute the case. But when the case came up and was put up for examination at trial, it predictably fell to pieces. I say "predictably" because it had been predicted by her own lawyers. There were five witnesses put forward at the original trial who gave direct evidence against Ramush Haradinaj. Four of them testified at the first trial. In the case of two of those four, the Trial Chamber found them to be wholly unreliable on core aspects of their evidence, namely, the supposed identification of Mr. Haradinaj, and reflected that in the judgement. And in the case of the other two, the Trial Chamber having heard their evidence in chief declined even to allow it to remain on the record because they were so demonstrably unreliable and their allegations and evidence so fantastic that their testimony had to be interrupted by the Trial Chamber and stopped before they could even be subjected to cross-examination. That is the type of material that this corrupted Serbian investigation generated and still generates. Neither of those two witnesses, I'm pleased to say, are relied on by the Prosecution in this re-trial, but it must be the case, therefore, that they accept that two of the witnesses that they put up as direct -- giving direct testimony against Mr. Haradinaj at the original trial were witnesses who could not conceivably be considered reliable witnesses of truth, two of a very small number. So it was in that context of a case so limpingly and appallingly put together and based on such flimsy and wholly unreliable evidence that the original Trial Chamber came to consider the evidence of the fifth witness who gave evidence against Mr. Haradinaj. The man who we know as Witness X. He was number five and he did not in fact testify. I'm going to return to him in a moment or two. As the Prosecution case inevitably unravelled last time round, it became clearer and clearer that there was no case for Mr. Haradinaj to answer. The Defence accordingly called no Defence evidence, another unique feature of these proceedings. In acquitting Mr. Haradinaj of all charges and finding that the JCE alleged against him then, and still alleged against him, did not exist at all, the original Trial Chamber effectively agreed that there never was a case for him to answer. There could, we say, be no clearer endorsement of Mr. Haradinaj's innocence than an acquittal by a Trial Chamber in the absence of any need to mount a Defence case at all. The Appeals Chamber in its judgement took a different view, holding that the absence of two crucial witnesses - I won't name them - had fatally undermined the original Trial Chamber's verdict, not as regards the JCE as a whole, but solely as regards to six counts concerned with Jabllanice. That decision came as a surprise to all concerned, not least to the Prosecution themselves. They had not been in a position before the Appeals Chamber even to assert that either of those witnesses would be willing to testify at any potential re-trial. Surprising, therefore, that such a re-trial should be ordered on that basis, but a surprise as much to the Prosecution as to the Defence. And yet here we are once again predictably enough in exactly the same position all over again with neither of those two witnesses currently indicating a willingness to testify. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Shefqet Kabashi has indicated that for principled reasons he does not wish to testify in these proceedings. He has made it clear over and over again that his unwillingness to testify is not because he is afraid of anyone and not because anyone has offered him any kind of inducement. It is because he does not consider that the Prosecution has acted fairly. More importantly, even if he were to testify, his statements do not make any allegation of criminal conduct at all against Mr. Haradinaj. Indeed, in his latest interview with Mr. Rogers, he complained loudly and vociferously about the injustice of putting Mr. Haradinaj on trial all over again. He was given numerous opportunities to testify at the original trial, but steadfastly maintained that he didn't want to participate and wasn't prepared to do so. We will see tomorrow whether anything has changed. The important point, though, in his case is that he made his own choice for his own reasons, reasons which have nothing to do with any fear or any alleged intimidation. (redacted) I apologise, can I ask for a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have a redaction, please. Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness X is a very different kettle of fish. The Prosecution, as I indicated, relies on statements that that witness made which include direct allegations of -- concerning the acts and conducts of Mr. Haradinaj across several of the counts on the amended indictment. Like Shefqet Kabashi this man was also given multiple opportunities to testify at the original trial and he came up with a veritable smorgasbord of reasons why he shouldn't be required to do so. Arrangements were made for him to give evidence via compelled videolink, but he steadfastly refused to come and testify. In his case, Your Honours, we say there are very strong motivations for him not to want to give evidence. That's not because of any genuine fear of the consequences of telling the truth, but because the whole of his testimony is a demonstrable series of lies. There are overwhelming challenges to the credibility of the inconsistent accounts he's given, not least of which is that a key witness, Witness 6, on whom Mr. Rogers places heavy reliance and who was at Jabllanice throughout the six-week period and who was shown a photograph of Witness X, was completely categorical that he had never been there during the time that he claims he was detained in the same room in which Witness 6 claimed he was detained. Another witness who's been mentioned -- another individual who's been mentioned by Mr. Rogers and who gave evidence at the previous trial is a man called Fadil Fazliu who's cited as a victim in Count 6. He testified last time round that the allegations made by Witness X, which he would have been present at, had they occurred, simply did not happen. How does the Prosecution respond? How does a fair Prosecutor respond? They just drop Fadil Fazliu from their witness list because it doesn't fit in with their case. It would be a matter for Your Honours to consider how to redress that obvious unfairness, but he's cited as a victim and Mr. Rogers doesn't have the courage to put him in the witness box. Not only that, there is incontrovertible forensic evidence that establishes beyond the peradventure that the allegations that Witness X makes simply cannot be true. I'm not going to elaborate the details in opening, but there is forensic -- independent forensic expert evidence about the manner in which certain injuries could have been inflicted which give an unequivocal lie to the central allegations that this man has made, no surprise then that he is less than keen to make them on oath in front of an international tribunal. Your Honours, there are very many reasons, it doesn't take me to point this out, there are very many reasons why a witness might choose not to testify. One possible reason, of course, is that they are genuinely afraid of telling the truth. There is no suggestion, though, and I want to underline this, and I will come back to it, despite some of the rumours and labels that have been attached to this trial, there is no suggestion - and never has been - that Mr. Haradinaj has ever been responsible for intimidating any witness, directly or indirectly, and there have been repeated judicial findings in the proceedings to date to the effect that he has not. Notwithstanding that fact, a view has gained currency that the original trial was flawed by intimidation. There are, as we say, and I don't need to labour the point, many other reasons why a witness like Witness X might not want to give evidence on oath in support of statements he's made to the Prosecution, foremost amongst these, of course, is his realisation that he's lied and that his lies will be exposed before the world. That is the position, we say, with Witness X. He has prevaricated throughout about testifying and given a range of reasons why he's not willing to do so, but the real reason will become clear if he ever does finally testify, because if he does give evidence, an outcome which is still open to very serious doubt in view of his previous conduct and his current stated position, he will, we say, be exposed as a liar and a perjurer. In short, we are beginning this re-trial precisely where the original trial left off. I'm going to ask for what I'm about to say to be redacted is probably the easiest way of doing it rather than going into closed session because it's a sentence or two. Very well, closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, are you asking for closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please have a closed session -- private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So far as Mr. Haradinaj is concerned, there is only one witness who makes any allegations against him, and that is Witness 81. This witness was first put in contact with the Prosecution in October 2010, that is more than two and a half years after Mr. Haradinaj's acquittal. By the time he gave his first account, the allegations made by the Prosecution and made on the basis of Witness X's evidence had been very widely reported and were publicly known. They were well-known and easy to mimic, and yet in the detail it is clear that the attempt at mimicry has failed. It's another extraordinary feature of this case that supposedly out of the blue and after its appeal, the Prosecution now has a new witness brought to its attention who purports to corroborate Witness 80. Mr. Rogers rightly recognises, because he knows what's coming, that there are major inconsistencies. Well, I'm -- see, this is the difficulty because Mr. Rogers in open session has made the point that I've just made without any concern, namely, that it's a corroborating witness of Witness 80. I'm afraid I'm being held to a completely variable and unworkable standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. We know why we did what we did earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The timing and circumstances in which Witness 81 came to the attention of the Office of the Prosecutor cast very serious doubts on his integrity and credibility. As Mr. Rogers acknowledges and as we would put it, his statements are riddled with inconsistencies, and he makes assertions throughout that are demonstrably false. But all that is a matter for cross-examination if he attends. But it is right that at the outset that Your Honours should know what kind of man he is. This witness, the only witness who is currently expected to testify against Mr. Haradinaj in this re-trial, is a man with a lengthy criminal record, including numerous offences of dishonesty, who has been found by an international tribunal to be a wholly unreliable Prosecution witness. In a prosecution in Kosovo, and I won't mention it in order risking identifying him, in a prosecution in Kosovo before international judges appointed by UNMIK, he made a statement, complainant statement, alleging that he had been seriously mistreated and abducted. His statements to the investigating judge were at first instance admitted at trial and he was not required to give evidence viva voce because he claimed that he had been intimidated. That well illustrates the danger, if I may say so, of taking allegations of intimidation at face value coming, as they do, from tainted witnesses. Because on appeal to the Supreme Court of Kosovo, again comprised of international judges appointed by the UN, it was found, we say, inevitably that his statements were not credible and a re-trial was ordered to assure that he could be cross-examined and give evidence viva voce. At that point, the Prosecutor withdrew the charges rather than proceed in reliance on his testimony. Other witnesses in the same trial alleged that their evidence had been actively manipulated by the Serb police, a feature which, as we shall see, has also beset this investigation and these proceedings. Your Honours should also know that one of his previous criminal convictions is for making false allegations of criminal conduct to the police; in other words, attempting to pervert the course of justice. He has form, in other words, for lying to the authorities at least twice and to the court at least once in an effort to procure a conviction of another. Precisely what we say he is doing here. It is, Your Honours, most surprising that a responsible Prosecutor is prepared to rely on that sort of evidence before an international criminal court and to stake its reputation on such a dubious witness. It is all the more surprising if, as now seems likely, he ends up being the only witness in relation to Mr. Haradinaj upon whom the Prosecution can directly rely. He is the sort of witness, Your Honours, upon whom one simply would not hang a cat. Since the inception of these proceedings, the Prosecution has sought to hide behind bogus allegations of witness intimidation made by wholly unreliable witnesses like this man as a pretext to conceal the evidential shortcomings in a prosecution that should never have been brought in the first place. There is, it appears, every reason and indication to believe that Mr. Rogers intends to continue in that tradition. For the rest of the charges, Your Honour, the Prosecution relies on the same vague JCE that was found not proven in the original trial. I want just to say a word or two, if I may, about the content of the material that that then gives rise to. There are really three broad categories, and they have each been mentioned with different degrees of diffidence. The first is the material that's going to be put before you by the "head of analytical department of the RDB," Serbian intelligence services, a man called Zoran Stijovic. To the chagrin, surprise, of the previous Trial Chamber, this man admitted in answers to me -- to questions from me and from Judge Orie that the methodology used to obtain the sort of material Mr. Rogers wants you to look at includes torture, blackmail, and bribery, informants who were either ill-treated or threatened or bribed or very often blackmailed; in other words, put into a sexually compromising position and then exploited. Much of the material is anonymous. Mr. Rogers in the end said to you, well, it's there for what it's worth. It's hard to imagine a Prosecutor putting it with less enthusiasm. It's there for what it's worth. Well, I'll tell you what it's worth, if I may, it's worth nothing. Secondly, KLA communiqués. It's suggested that you ought to draw an inference of a joint criminal enterprise involving Mr. Haradinaj from the publication of KLA communiqués. In order to understand how this works, it's necessary to look at some of the material about how the Kosovo Liberation Army started to come into existence, but the so-called General Staff was an organisation loosely comprised of individuals mainly based outside Kosovo who had very little connection with officers or officials on the ground and certainly was not directly issuing commands or the subject of any command structure in relation to the Kosovo Liberation Army in western Kosovo and in the Dukagjin region generally. Their press spokesman was a man called Jakup Krasniqi, who gave evidence at the previous trial, and who is the author of these communiqués. None of these documents were authored by Mr. Haradinaj or issued on his authority. They don't reflect the policy of Mr. Haradinaj or of the KLA in the Dukagjin area, and none of the communiqués relates to any alleged incident on the indictment in relation to Jabllanice. Evidence about the communiqués was given at trial which led to serious doubts about their reliability and the accuracy of their contents. And the original Trial Chamber found them to be unreliable propaganda tools which frequently exaggerated successes and minimised set-backs and failures and that's why they found, as we will invite you to find, that no policy of kidnapping, killing, or mistreating civilians can be inferred from that material and certainly nothing which could conceivably be linked to Mr. Haradinaj, who did not operate within a command structure issued -- or instructions or communiqués issued by the so-called self-styled General Staff. Black lists was the third examples that Mr. Rogers gave you. He suggested that there was good evidence of the KLA maintaining black lists of targeted civilians, and he told you that you would be entitled to consider the testimony of Witness 17 who received a black list containing a list of names, including the name of Skender Kuci, one of the victims in the six counts and whose remains were subsequently found. Witness 17 was the head of a brigade of soldiers who entered Kosovo under the banner of the FARK, the F-A-R-K. They were an independent army from the Kosovo Liberation Army and there was a period of time during which there were conflicts between the two groupings after the FARK entered across the mountains from Albania into Kosovo. Thereafter, thereafter there was a process of integration, although a rather unhappy truce and alliance existed between the two. The barracks at Baran, which is to the north of the area shown as being within the four subzones, was commanded by Witness 17 on behalf of FARK. Nothing, as it happens, directly to do with the separately operating Kosovo Liberation Army. He received at some point a list of names. He doesn't know who gave it to him, he says. He doesn't know what its purpose was, he says. He didn't even know where it had come from or when he had received it, but one thing he was sure of is he never brought it to Ramush Haradinaj's attention and it certainly didn't come from him or through him or anyone associated with him. So what are we left with? A man's got a list and on the list is a name of a victim who it appears was detained at Jabllanice and subsequently died. But who is that victim? That victim is Skender Kuci. Skender Kuci is the man who Rrustem Tetaj informed Ramush Haradinaj was being detained and who Ramush Haradinaj immediately travelled across the zone in order to secure the release of. Hardly, we say, consistent with an allegation of joint criminal enterprise. It is no surprise, Your Honours, that lawyers advised this case shouldn't be brought and no surprise that the previous Trial Chamber dismissed it. There are as well considerable areas of evidence upon which the Prosecution is proposing to rely at which, in our submission, are wholly irrelevant for the limited issues that you have to consider concerning Jabllanice on the opposite side of the Dukagjin zone. First of all, there is a section of the Prosecution's opening brief and an indication that they intend to rely upon an incident on the 18th of April in Gllogjan in which members of the Stojanovic family were beaten by a mob, if I can put it that way. Those allegations formed the basis of Counts 3 and 4 of the original indictment upon which Mr. Haradinaj was acquitted. It's an allegation that predates the agreed date of the start of armed conflict and is not therefore subject, in any event, to the requirements of international humanitarian law. It has nothing whatsoever to do with Jabllanice. It's far removed in space and time from any of the allegations on this indictment. It can't be relied upon as evidence of system or bad character because the Prosecution accepts Mr. Haradinaj was acquitted of it and that is res judicata, and it was in any event a spontaneous attack by local villagers in response to the fact that the Serb forces had used the Stojanovic family home as a military facility in order to launch an attack which resulted in the death of three teenagers and a vast amount of damage and injury in the village of Gllogjan. It has got nothing to do with this case but once again because the Prosecution is driven at this stage to try to put anything it can together, they are scraping the barrel. Another classic example. FARK, I've already indicated the background. FARK entered Kosovo from Albania. There was a period of conflict and a number of incidents of conflict between the two forces immediately after FARK brigades came in. They were eventually resolved with the two forces integrating and distributing responsibility, and out of all of that complex background the Prosecution have selected a single incident on the 4th of July, again in Gllogjan and Irzniq, on the opposite side of the Dukagjin zone from Jabllanice, in which it is said that there was a confrontation and one of the FARK soldiers was shot. Well, if -- even if that's right, the reason you find no reference to it in the original Trial Chamber's judgement is because it's got nothing to do with the allegations on this indictment. It's a desperate stuff -- it's got nothing to do with the allegations on the indictment because ti has got nothing to do with civilians or opponents. It was, if anything, part of a military conflict between two armed forces and it's got absolutely nothing to do with the detention of civilians or others at Jabllanice occurring, as it allegedly did, many miles away in Gllogjan. Part of the conflict between two Kosovar Albanian armed forces many miles removed. So nothing, we say, to do with this case. But a clumsy attempt to clutch at straws precisely because the Prosecution has no credible evidence that Mr. Haradinaj ever participated in, authorised, condoned any of the crimes against civilians that are alleged to have been committed at Jabllanice and that is what this partial re-trial is truly all about. As Your Honours know, there's plenty of evidence from the original trial about command structures within the KLA during this early period of its development. I just want to draw up four short themes in the time that remains. First of all, the evidence shows that in the period of the indictment the KLA was struggling to establish itself. During the first half of 1998 it was made up of a small number of committed fighters like Mr. Haradinaj together with a much larger number of ill-trained, ill-equipped volunteers, village guards. The essential point as I opened at the very outset is that its structure was horizontal not vertical, that's why there is no allegation under Article 7(3) of the Statute. At that point in its history, the KLA lacked any formal or effective command structure and the attempt that Mr. Rogers has made to lay at the door of Ramush Haradinaj, commander at the opposite side of the Dukagjin zone, crimes that were allegedly committed in his absence inside Jabllanice is feeble. Most of those who fought for the KLA were villagers who returned to their daily lives when they weren't involved in the fighting, fighters by night, farmers by day. And as it's said by one of the witnesses in the original trial, Mr. Haradinaj was in reality the commander of those who chose on any particular day to follow him. The level of co-ordination between the different villages where the KLA was able to set up village defences was minimal. It has to be taken into account that all of this took place during repeated Serbian offences into the area with which we are concerned. One of the points of interest in Mr. Rogers' opening was his suggestion that there was a free area within which the KLA was effectively free to operate. In the original trial the Prosecution called that an area of total control and they relied on that map by Colonel John Crosland to establish what the boundaries of that total area of control were until Mr. Crosland gave evidence of course, and when he gave evidence - and assuming Mr. Rogers has actually read the transcript he will know what it was that Colonel Crosland actually said, which is that it would be completely inappropriate to make the suggestion that the boundary he had drawn represented an area of total control. On the contrary he said -- and just to find out the precise terms: "Paramilitaries used to terrify the civilian population from the Bosnian war stationed in Gjakove and Peje. I would have been surprised if those forces hadn't entered the zone like flies to a jam pot." So, we're dealing with a situation which was porous, where there were conflicts involving Serb forces, very poorly armed, very poorly trained, not trained at all in effect, village volunteers, struggling to create some sort of co-ordinated structure. That is the context in which Mr. Rogers wants you to hold Mr. Haradinaj responsible for crimes that were committed in his absence in a facility on the opposite side of the Dukagjin zone over which he was not the effective commander. The evidence, Your Honours, shows that there was certainly no common agreement in respect of commissions of -- the commission of crimes in detention facilities by the KLA at all and certainly no such agreement in relation to Jabllanice. Leaving those two witnesses aside, X and 81, there is no direct evidence at all implicating Mr. Haradinaj. He was on the evidence hardly ever there. He certainly did not exercise day-to-day effective command and control, and of the three witnesses who did testify to his direct intervention, one was Rrustem Tetaj, who testified to his intervention in Jabllanice in order to secure the release of an injured person who'd been wrongly detained there, the second was Witness 3 who said they -- ill-treated at Jabllanice. When he arrived at Gllogjan, he was protected and given a treatment to ensure he was never ill-treated again. And the third, another desperate attempt by the Prosecution, relates to a man called Achilleas Pappas, who was a member of the European Community Monitoring Mission, who was briefly detained on the opposite side of the zone from Jabllanice, as he was driving into a war zone. In other words, there was a Serbian offensive going on on the day and he drove in a Land Rover directly into the line of fire. He was stopped by KLA soldiers and treated in a manner which, on his description, was inappropriate, rough-handled, and rude, until Mr. Haradinaj turned up. And as soon as he turned up, Mr. Pappas was treated with complete courtesy and professionalism, and in his own words given a proper handling and sent safely on his way, and he described Mr. Haradinaj as having been professional in his dealings with him throughout. Your Honours, as a soldier, we make no secret of the fact that Mr. Haradinaj was hard, brave, and effective. His targets were combatants, not civilians. Faced with the overwhelming fire-power of the Serbian forces, he and others managed to put together, to cobble together, a force sufficient to defend civilian enclaves in an area which was subject to a Serbian, effectively, scorched-earth policy. He led always by example and never expected anyone to fight battles he wasn't prepared to fight himself. He managed to fight off with a handful of people the Serbian offensive on Gllogjan which has become known as one of the key moments in the Kosovar struggle for liberation from the domination of Serbia. But as you will hear from any witness of credibility, he is, was, and always has been a fighter of honour. The targeting of civilians was never one of Mr. Haradinaj's military objectives, and he never ordered or condoned the ill-treatment of detainees. That sort of dishonourable conduct is the very antithesis of the principles which have guided him. As prime minister of Kosovo after the war, he was widely praised by the international community for his hundred days in office. He was regarded as a leader who genuinely reached out to the Serbian population, who sought to forge a common and integrated future for Kosovo, but his time in office was cut short by the OTP's indictment, just as the Serbian authorities intended that it should be. He resigned immediately the indictment was issued and he voluntarily surrendered himself to the ICTY, in stark contrast as the Trial Chamber at the time noted, to the attitude of other leaders who'd been indicted by this Tribunal. And it's interesting as we start to move into the evidence, it's just interesting to ask Your Honours to bear this in mind. This is a man who believed and fought for his country's statehood. He believed and fought for it to the point of making ultimate personal sacrifices. He carried the body of his own brother 17 miles over the mountains from Kosovo into Albania when he'd been shot by the Serbian forces. His family have made huge sacrifices for Kosovar statehood, and it's in recognition of that statehood that when called upon to answer to charges before a serious international tribunal, he immediately resigned, called for calm on the streets of Kosovo, completed his parliamentary obligations for the morning and flew to The Hague. Not surprisingly he gained credit for that. He was released on provisional release and continued in full conformity with the requirements of the Trial Chamber to exercise only political activity in private. Now, I say that because his commitment and the respect that he's shown to this Tribunal deserve reciprocation. We're in a situation now where a real shoddy re-trial is being mounted and we would ask Your Honours to approach it with the robustness that it deserves. Mr. Haradinaj's respect stands in the starkest possible contrast to the way in which the Prosecution has conducted itself. Putting forward witnesses like Witness X who haven't even shown this court the time of day and have refused orders to testify or make themselves available for cross-examination because they want to hide behind their lies. Despite the fact that they've made very serious allegations against an honourable political leader. Your Honours, we respectfully submit - and I don't want to cause the need to go back into open session - but we respectfully submit that there are two witnesses in relation to these proceedings without whom we would not be here at all. No doubt faced with the background of the previous Trial Chamber's frustration at the endless continuing prevarication, Your Honours will do what the Appeals Chamber directed should be done and give those witnesses a fair opportunity to testify. But to depart from legal language for a moment, enough is enough. The credibility of this Tribunal depends on a robust trial here. These two witnesses should not be permitted to wag the dog, so to speak, and to hold up these proceedings indefinitely to keep Mr. Haradinaj further in custody. Bring them on we say. Those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. We note the time. I guess this is an appropriate time and a convenient time to break up for today. The matter stands adjourned until tomorrow afternoon, 2.15, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of August, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.
